entries.test_step: Create a custom role 'editor_plus' with caps ['edit_posts','delete_posts']. Write code with in_array('administrator', \$user->roles). Assign 'editor_plus' to a test user. Verify deletion fails (wrong role name) — this is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('delete_posts'). Verify deletion now works.

entries.title: WordPress: current_user_can() expects a capability, not a role name — use manage_options not administrator
entries.summary: current_user_can() expects a capability slug (manage_options, edit_posts, delete_posts) — not a role name (administrator, editor). WordPress has a backward-compatibility fallback that treats role names as pseudo-capabilities on single sites, but it is unreliable on multisite and with custom role configurations. AI code frequently passes role names, producing code that silently fails in production configurations that differ from localhost.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — use capabilities, not role names
if ( current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) {
    update_option( 'site_settings', $settings );
}

if ( current_user_can( 'publish_posts' ) ) {
    wp_publish_post( $post_id );
}

if ( current_user_can( 'edit_others_posts' ) ) {
    // Grants access to editor AND administrator (and any role with that cap)
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — 'administrator' is a role name, not a capability
if ( current_user_can( 'administrator' ) ) {
    update_option( 'site_settings', $settings );
}

// WRONG — 'editor' is a role name
if ( current_user_can( 'editor' ) ) {
    wp_publish_post( $post_id );
}
entries.test_step: Create a custom role 'super_admin' with manage_options cap but not named 'administrator'. Write code: if (current_user_can('administrator')). Assign 'super_admin' to a test user. Verify check fails (role name mismatch) — this is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('manage_options'). Verify check passes.

entries.title: WordPress: is_admin() checks the URL context, not user permissions — use current_user_can() for authorization
entries.summary: is_admin() returns true whenever the current request targets the wp-admin/ area — including unauthenticated AJAX requests to wp-admin/admin-ajax.php. It does NOT check whether the current user has administrator privileges. Using is_admin() as a security gate allows any subscriber who triggers an admin-ajax.php request to pass the check and execute privileged code.
entries.code_example:
403 ] ); } } ); // CORRECT — combine for admin-only UI with security gate add_action( 'admin_notices', function() { if ( is_admin() && current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) { echo '

Admin notice.

'; } } ); // CORRECT — AJAX endpoint properly gated add_action( 'wp_ajax_my_action', function() { check_ajax_referer( 'my_nonce' ); if ( ! current_user_can( 'edit_posts' ) ) { wp_send_json_error( 'Insufficient permissions', 403 ); } wp_send_json_success( [ 'result' => 'ok' ] ); } );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — is_admin() is not an authorization check
add_action( 'wp_loaded', function() {
    if ( is_admin() ) {
        // A subscriber with access to admin-ajax.php passes this check
        update_option( 'site_config', $_POST['config'] );
    }
} );
entries.test_step: Create a subscriber user. Write code: if ( is_admin() ) { update_option('secret', 'value'); }. Make an authenticated AJAX request from that subscriber to wp-admin/admin-ajax.php. Verify is_admin() returns true and option is updated — this is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('manage_options'). Repeat — option is not updated.

entries.title: WordPress: use wp_remote_get() / wp_remote_post() instead of raw curl_* or file_get_contents()
entries.summary: Raw curl_init() / curl_exec() calls inside WordPress code bypass the HTTP API (wp_remote_get, wp_remote_post). The WordPress HTTP API provides: unified timeout control, proxy/firewall compatibility, WP_Error on failure, SSL verification, and compatibility with object cache layers. curl_* gives you none of these. It also does not respect the WordPress 'http_api_transports' filter or the REQUESTS_SILENCE_PSR0_DEPRECATIONS constant. Use wp_remote_get() / wp_remote_post() for all HTTP requests inside WordPress.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — WordPress HTTP API with error handling
$response = wp_remote_get(
    'https://api.example.com/data',
    [ 'timeout' => 10 ]
);

if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
    error_log( 'HTTP error: ' . $response->get_error_message() );
    return null;
}

$status = wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response );
if ( 200 !== $status ) {
    error_log( "API returned HTTP {$status}" );
    return null;
}

$body = wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response );
$data = json_decode( $body, true );

// For user-provided URLs (prevents SSRF):
$safe_response = wp_safe_remote_get( $user_url, [ 'timeout' => 10 ] );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — raw curl, no timeout, no WP_Error integration
$ch = curl_init( 'https://api.example.com/data' );
curl_setopt( $ch, CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER, true );
$response = curl_exec( $ch );
curl_close( $ch );
$data = json_decode( $response, true );
// $response could be false on failure — no check
entries.test_step: Write code using curl_init / curl_exec targeting a slow endpoint (30-second delay). Verify it blocks the page load with no timeout. Replace with wp_remote_get($url, ['timeout' => 10]). Repeat — page load completes in 10 seconds; WP_Error is caught.

entries.title: WordPress HTTP API: always check is_wp_error() before accessing wp_remote_* response body
entries.summary: wp_remote_get(), wp_remote_post(), and similar functions return either an array (success) or a WP_Error (DNS failure, timeout, SSL error, connection refused). AI code frequently omits the is_wp_error() check, directly accessing \$response['body'] — which causes 'Cannot access offset on WP_Error' fatal errors whenever the remote server is unreachable. Always check is_wp_error() before accessing the response.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — guard with is_wp_error() before any access
$response = wp_remote_get(
    'https://api.example.com/data',
    [ 'timeout' => 10 ]
);

if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
    $error_code = $response->get_error_code();
    $error_msg  = $response->get_error_message();
    error_log( "Failed to fetch API: {$error_code} — {$error_msg}" );
    return null;
}

$status = wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response );
if ( 200 !== $status ) {
    error_log( "API returned HTTP {$status}" );
    return null;
}

$body = wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response );
$data = json_decode( $body, true );

return $data['key'] ?? null;
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — assumes $response is always an array
$response = wp_remote_get( 'https://api.example.com/data' );
$body = $response['body'];  // Fatal: Cannot access offset on WP_Error
$data = json_decode( $body, true );
echo $data['status'];  // Never reached if network fails
entries.test_step: Write code: \$response = wp_remote_get(\$url); \$body = \$response['body']; Kill the remote server or block DNS. Call the code — verify fatal PHP error 'Cannot access offset on WP_Error'. Add is_wp_error() guard. Repeat — no fatal; error is logged gracefully.

entries.title: WordPress options: set autoload=false for large or rarely-accessed options to prevent alloptions bloat
entries.summary: add_option() defaults to autoload='yes'. Every autoloaded option is fetched and held in memory on every WordPress page load via wp_load_alloptions(), even if the page never uses the option. Large options — JSON-encoded arrays, serialized post lists, or any value over ~1KB — cause measurable memory overhead per request. Use the fourth parameter to set autoload=false for options accessed rarely or only on specific admin pages.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — large option with autoload=false
add_option(
    'my_plugin_large_config',
    [
        'data'  => json_encode( expensive_dataset() ),
        'posts' => get_posts( [ 'numberposts' => 500 ] ),
    ],
    '',
    false  // autoload=false: only fetched when get_option() is called explicitly
);

// Fetch on demand (single query, only when needed)
$config = get_option( 'my_plugin_large_config' );

// Small option — autoload=true is fine
add_option(
    'my_plugin_version',
    '1.0.0',
    '',
    true  // tiny string, accessed on every page — OK to autoload
);
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — large option, autoloaded by default on every page
add_option( 'my_plugin_large_config', [
    'data'  => json_encode( expensive_dataset() ),
    'posts' => get_posts( [ 'numberposts' => 500 ] ),
] );
// Every page load: +5MB memory, +extra DB query for alloptions
entries.test_step: Add a large option with default autoload: add_option('big_data', json_encode(array_fill(0,1000,'x'))). Use Query Monitor to observe wp_load_alloptions() on a page that doesn't use this option — the big_data row is always loaded. Re-add with autoload=false. Verify the row no longer appears in alloptions on unrelated pages.

entries.title: WordPress transients: get_transient() returns false on expiry — always check and regenerate
entries.summary: get_transient() returns false when the transient has expired, was deleted, or was never set. AI code frequently assigns the result directly and accesses properties or array keys on it — causing 'Cannot access offset on bool' fatal errors when the cache misses. The pattern requires an explicit false check and a regeneration fallback. Without it, the code is also vulnerable to cache stampede: many simultaneous requests all regenerate the expensive value at once when the transient expires.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — strict false check with regeneration fallback
function get_api_data() {
    $data = get_transient( 'my_api_data' );

    if ( false === $data ) {
        $response = wp_remote_get( 'https://api.example.com/data', [ 'timeout' => 10 ] );

        if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
            return null;  // Graceful fallback on network error
        }

        $data = json_decode( wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response ), true );
        set_transient( 'my_api_data', $data, HOUR_IN_SECONDS );
    }

    return $data['key'] ?? null;
}

// CORRECT — strict false check preserves 0 and '' as valid cached values
$count = get_transient( 'my_post_count' );
if ( false === $count ) {
    $count = count_all_posts();  // 0 is a valid count
    set_transient( 'my_post_count', $count, DAY_IN_SECONDS );
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — assumes transient always exists
function get_api_data() {
    $data = get_transient( 'my_api_data' );
    // $data is false if expired or never set
    return $data['key'];  // Fatal: Cannot access offset 'key' on false
}

// ALSO WRONG — loose check misses valid falsy cached values
$data = get_transient( 'my_count' );
if ( ! $data ) {  // Re-generates when cached value is 0 or ''
    $data = count_all_posts();
    set_transient( 'my_count', $data, DAY_IN_SECONDS );
}
entries.test_step: Write code: \$data = get_transient('test'); echo \$data['key']; Set and then delete the transient. Call the code — verify fatal PHP error 'Cannot access offset on bool false'. Add if ( false === \$data ) { regenerate... }. Repeat — no error; fallback triggers and data is regenerated.

entries.title: WordPress cron: wp_schedule_event() only fires on page load — use system cron for time-critical jobs
entries.summary: wp_schedule_event() registers a task in the database but does NOT run it independently. The task fires only when a visitor loads the site AND the scheduled time has passed. On low-traffic sites — staging environments, B2B tools, overnight jobs — no page load means no task execution. Using wp-cron for payment processing, webhook delivery, or time-sensitive notifications causes silent delays or complete misses. For reliable scheduling, disable wp-cron (DISABLE_WP_CRON=true) and use a real system cron job to trigger wp-cron.php.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT for non-critical tasks — wp-cron alone is fine
add_action( 'init', function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_nightly_summary' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'daily', 'my_nightly_summary' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_nightly_summary', function() {
    $summary = generate_daily_summary();
    wp_mail( get_option( 'admin_email' ), 'Daily Summary', $summary );
} );

// CORRECT for critical tasks: disable wp-cron + system cron
// wp-config.php:
// define( 'DISABLE_WP_CRON', true );

// crontab (guaranteed trigger):
// * * * * * curl -s https://example.com/wp-cron.php?doing_wp_cron >/dev/null 2>&1

// The hook registration stays the same:
add_action( 'my_payment_check', function() {
    $pending = get_option( 'pending_payments', [] );
    foreach ( $pending as $payment ) {
        process_payment( $payment );  // Now runs reliably every minute
    }
} );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — wp-cron is not a reliable scheduler for payment processing
add_action( 'init', function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_payment_check' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'hourly', 'my_payment_check' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_payment_check', function() {
    $pending = get_option( 'pending_payments', [] );
    foreach ( $pending as $payment ) {
        process_payment( $payment );  // Must run every hour — but won't if no visitors
    }
} );
entries.test_step: Schedule a task to run every hour. Wait 2 hours without loading the site. Check if the task ran (e.g., count in wp_options) — it hasn't. Load the site once — task runs immediately. This demonstrates the traffic dependency. Fix: add DISABLE_WP_CRON=true + system cron. Wait 2 hours without loading the site — task now runs on schedule.

entries.title: WordPress cron: scheduled events survive plugin deactivation — add register_deactivation_hook with wp_unschedule_event()
entries.summary: WordPress stores scheduled events in wp_options. Deactivating a plugin does not remove its events — they persist indefinitely, showing up in Site Health as orphaned events. When wp-cron fires an orphaned event, it looks for the callback, finds nothing, and silently fails. Always pair register_activation_hook() (which schedules events) with register_deactivation_hook() that calls wp_unschedule_event() or wp_clear_scheduled_hook() to remove them.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — schedule on activation, clean up on deactivation
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_weekly_report' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'weekly', 'my_weekly_report' );
    }
} );

register_deactivation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    // wp_clear_scheduled_hook removes ALL scheduled instances of this hook
    wp_clear_scheduled_hook( 'my_weekly_report' );
} );

add_action( 'my_weekly_report', function() {
    send_admin_email( 'Weekly Report', generate_report() );
} );

// Test: deactivate plugin, then:
// wp cron event list | grep my_weekly_report
// → should return nothing
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — schedules event on activation, no cleanup on deactivation
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_weekly_report' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'weekly', 'my_weekly_report' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_weekly_report', function() {
    send_admin_email( 'Weekly Report', generate_report() );
} );
// After plugin deactivation: event stays in wp_options forever
entries.test_step: Activate plugin that schedules cron event. Run: wp cron event list. Deactivate plugin (without cleanup code). Run: wp cron event list again — event is still listed. Add register_deactivation_hook with wp_clear_scheduled_hook. Deactivate again — event is now gone.

entries.title: Non-negotiable folder layout for every WordPress project
entries.summary: Every professional WordPress project, large or small, needs the same folder building blocks: a codebase directory separate from core, a mu-plugins folder, a vendor directory managed by Composer, a config directory, a tests directory, a bin directory for scripts, plus .gitignore, .env.example, and README.md. Without this baseline you lose instant orientation and end up reinventing structure on every project.
entries.code_example:
# Standard project layout
my-wp-project/
├── app/                   # or wp-content/ depending on setup
│   ├── mu-plugins/        # always-on core logic
│   ├── plugins/           # feature plugins (Composer-managed)
│   └── themes/            # presentation only
├── config/                # environment config files
├── tests/                 # automated tests
├── bin/                   # scaffold.sh, setup scripts
├── vendor/                # Composer autoload output — never edit
├── composer.json
├── composer.lock
├── .gitignore
├── .env.example
└── README.md
entries.bad_pattern:
# What an unstructured project looks like
my-wp-project/
├── wp-content/
│   └── themes/
│       └── my-theme/
│           ├── functions.php   # REST endpoints, CPTs, cron jobs, helpers — all mixed in
│           ├── api.php
│           └── helpers.php     # duplicated across themes
# No composer.json, no tests/, no config/, no README.md, no .env.example
entries.test_step: Open the project root. Can you immediately identify where the theme is, where plugin logic lives, and how to set up a new environment? If the answer requires opening multiple files to figure out — the structure is incomplete.

entries.title: Composer as the dependency backbone of a WordPress project
entries.summary: Composer is the central control center for every dependency in a professional WordPress project. You define what the project needs in composer.json, you get exactly those versions, you can update specific packages with composer update and track every change in Git, and the lockfile ensures everyone on the team gets the exact same version. ZIP-uploading plugins is not a professional workflow — it is technical debt.
entries.test_step: Run `composer validate` in the project root — it must exit 0. Run `composer install --no-dev` on a clean clone and confirm the project runs without manual file moves. Run `composer show` and verify every plugin/theme version matches what was committed to composer.lock.

entries.title: Commit composer.lock — reproducible builds depend on it
entries.summary: composer.lock is the source of truth for exactly which versions are installed across all machines and CI environments. Committing it ensures everyone on the team gets the exact same dependency tree. Without it, composer install resolves to different minor versions on different machines, which is how "works on my machine" bugs arrive. The lockfile belongs in Git — vendor/ does not.
entries.code_example:
# .gitignore — what to exclude
/vendor/
/.env
/wp/              # WordPress core installed by Composer

# composer.lock stays IN Git — never ignore it
# Run on CI / new clone:
composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader
entries.bad_pattern:
# composer.lock in .gitignore — reproducibility broken
/vendor/
/composer.lock    # WRONG — removes the pin on dependency versions

# Or: committing vendor/ to Git
git add vendor/   # WRONG — bloats history, causes merge conflicts on update
entries.test_step: Confirm composer.lock is tracked: `git ls-files composer.lock` must return composer.lock. Confirm vendor/ is ignored: `git ls-files vendor/` must return nothing. On a fresh clone run `composer install --no-dev` — it must succeed without network access to package metadata (the lock file satisfies it).

entries.title: Bedrock vs classic WordPress structure — the decision framework
entries.summary: Bedrock (roots.io/bedrock) restructures WordPress by using /web/ as the web root, requiring Composer for core + plugins + themes, and enforcing environment-based configuration via a .env file. It brings structure, but it also demands more: a deployment system, Composer-native workflows, and server control. The classic structure is not inferior — it is often used incorrectly. You do not need Bedrock to work professionally; you need structure and discipline.
entries.code_example:
# Install Bedrock via Composer
composer create-project roots/bedrock my-project
cd my-project

# Install a plugin via wpackagist
composer require wpackagist-plugin/query-monitor

# Bedrock reads config from .env — never hard-coded in wp-config.php
# .env example:
# DB_NAME=my_db
# DB_USER=my_user
# DB_PASSWORD=secret
# WP_HOME=https://my-project.test
# WP_SITEURL=https://my-project.test/wp
entries.bad_pattern:
# Mixing Bedrock with manual workflows — the worst of both worlds
# Using Bedrock but uploading a plugin via ZIP in wp-admin:
#   version not tracked in composer.lock
#   plugin sits in web/app/plugins/ but not in require block
#
# Using Bedrock but committing vendor/:
git add web/wp/   # WRONG — WP core is a Composer dependency, not your code
entries.test_step: If using Bedrock: run `composer install` on a clean clone, create the .env file from .env.example, and confirm `wp core version` returns the expected version. Confirm no plugins in web/app/plugins/ that are absent from composer.json. If using classic: confirm wp-config.php reads from a .env file or environment variables, not hard-coded credentials.

entries.title: WP-CLI as a scaffolding tool — automate project setup entirely
entries.summary: WP-CLI goes far beyond wp plugin install. You can automate complete project setups — installation, database creation, theme activation, plugin configuration, option setting, dummy content, permalink flushing — all in a single script that runs in under a minute, consistently, on every machine. Manual setup is not a speed problem; it is a system problem. Anything you do not automate becomes a recurring source of errors.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/scaffold.sh — one script to set up the full WP project

set -euo pipefail

PROJECT_NAME=${1:-my-project}
WP_ADMIN_USER=admin
WP_ADMIN_EMAIL=dev@example.com

# 1. Download WordPress core
wp core download --locale=en_US

# 2. Create wp-config.php from environment
wp config create \
  --dbname="${DB_NAME}" \
  --dbuser="${DB_USER}" \
  --dbpass="${DB_PASSWORD}" \
  --dbhost="db"

# 3. Create and populate the database
wp db create
wp core install \
  --url="https://${PROJECT_NAME}.test" \
  --title="${PROJECT_NAME}" \
  --admin_user="${WP_ADMIN_USER}" \
  --admin_email="${WP_ADMIN_EMAIL}" \
  --skip-email

# 4. Set common options
wp option update blogdescription ""
wp option update default_comment_status closed

# 5. Activate theme + plugins
wp theme activate my-theme
wp plugin activate my-plugin

# 6. Flush rewrite rules
wp rewrite structure "/%postname%/"
wp rewrite flush

echo "Done. Project ${PROJECT_NAME} is ready."
entries.bad_pattern:
# Anti-patterns in project setup
# 1. Copy-paste from last project:
cp -r ../old-project/wp-content/themes/old-theme ./wp-content/themes/new-theme
# carries over outdated config, stale functions.php snippets

# 2. Browser installer:
# Navigate to https://myproject.test/wp-admin/install.php and click through
# not reproducible, not documented, different settings every time

# 3. Manual plugin activation loop in wp-admin
# no record of which plugins were activated and in what order
entries.test_step: Run `wp cli version` to confirm WP-CLI is available. Then run your scaffold script on a fresh DDEV environment and confirm the site is fully configured — theme active, plugins active, permalinks set — with zero browser interaction.

entries.title: MU-plugins: the load-order-guaranteed foundation that cannot be switched off
entries.summary: WordPress loads files in /wp-content/mu-plugins/ before normal plugins, and there is no activate/deactivate toggle in the backend. This makes MU-plugins the right place for everything that must always run: security rules, project constants, logging and monitoring hooks, and health endpoints. One click on "Deactivate" in a normal plugin can take down security filters, logs, and health checks. That risk does not exist in MU-plugins.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// wp-content/mu-plugins/project-loader.php
// The MU-loader — loads project modules in a fixed, documented order.
// WordPress loads this file automatically before any normal plugin.

// 1. Project core: constants, helpers, CPT registration
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/constants.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/helpers.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/post-types.php';

// 2. Security: HTTPS enforcement, REST gates, XML-RPC off, header hygiene
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/security.php';

// 3. Audit: light trail for sensitive option changes (siteurl, admin_email)
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/audit.php';

// 4. API foundations: health-check endpoint always available
require_once __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/health-api.php';
entries.test_step: Confirm the mu-plugins directory exists: run `ls wp-content/mu-plugins/`. Log in to wp-admin and go to Plugins > Must-Use — confirm your MU-loader appears there and cannot be deactivated. Deactivate a normal plugin and confirm that security headers and health endpoints still respond correctly.

entries.title: MU-plugin autoloader — load subdirectory modules without manual require lists
entries.summary: WordPress only auto-loads PHP files directly in /wp-content/mu-plugins/ — it does not recurse into subdirectories. A small MU-loader in that directory uses require_once to load modules from subdirectories in a deliberate, fixed order. This keeps each concern in its own file while still guaranteeing load order. Version-control the loader and all modules as a unit; deploy via CI/CD or Composer from a private registry.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// wp-content/mu-plugins/project-loader.php
// Top-level loader — WordPress finds this automatically.
// Require modules in deliberate order from the project-core/ subdirectory.

defined('ABSPATH') || exit;

$core = __DIR__ . '/project-core/src/';

// Order matters: constants first, then security (needs constants), then features.
require_once $core . 'constants.php';
require_once $core . 'security.php';
require_once $core . 'post-types.php';
require_once $core . 'audit.php';
require_once $core . 'health-api.php';
entries.test_step: Add error_log("MU core loaded"); to your loader, then load any page. Confirm the message appears in the PHP error log. Verify that files in subdirectories (e.g. project-core/src/security.php) do NOT auto-load when the top-level loader is absent.

entries.title: Theme = presentation, Plugin = logic, MU-Plugin = always-on core
entries.summary: WordPress architecture has one non-negotiable rule: theme = presentation, plugin = logic, MU-plugin = always-on core. A theme is for layouts, styles, and template parts. Custom post types, API connections, cron jobs, and business logic belong in a plugin. Anything operational that must always run (security, constants, monitoring) belongs in an MU-plugin. Mixing these turns every relaunch into a rebuild.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT — Custom post type in a plugin, not a theme

// wp-content/plugins/my-events/src/PostTypes/EventPostType.php
namespace MyEvents\PostTypes;

class EventPostType {
    public function register(): void {
        register_post_type('event', [
            'labels'      => ['name' => 'Events', 'singular_name' => 'Event'],
            'public'      => true,
            'has_archive' => true,
            'rewrite'     => ['slug' => 'events'],
            'supports'    => ['title', 'editor', 'thumbnail'],
        ]);
    }
}

// In the plugin main file:
add_action('init', [new \MyEvents\PostTypes\EventPostType(), 'register']);
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG — business logic buried in functions.php (theme file)
// wp-content/themes/my-theme/functions.php

// Custom post type in theme — disappears on theme switch
add_action('init', function() {
    register_post_type('event', ['public' => true]);
});

// API connection in theme — tied to the old layout forever
add_action('init', function() {
    $response = wp_remote_get('https://api.example.com/events');
    // process and cache...
});

// Cron job in functions.php — stops running on theme switch
add_action('my_daily_sync', 'sync_remote_events');
if (!wp_next_scheduled('my_daily_sync')) {
    wp_schedule_event(time(), 'daily', 'my_daily_sync');
}
entries.test_step: Switch to a default WordPress theme (Twenty Twenty-Four). Do all custom post types, REST endpoints, and integrations still work? If anything breaks on theme switch, the logic is in the wrong place — move it to a plugin.

entries.title: Plugin skeleton — the internal structure every agency plugin must follow
entries.summary: Every plugin needs a clear purpose, and every agency should start from a skeleton that enforces internal structure. The required layout: src/ for classes (PSR-4 autoloaded), assets/ for CSS and JS, tests/ for unit tests, and composer.json for autoload configuration. That way any developer instantly knows where to look. Without a skeleton, every plugin eventually turns into a junkyard.
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// wp-content/plugins/my-plugin/my-plugin.php — 2000 lines, everything in one file

// CPT registration
function my_plugin_register_cpt() { /* ... */ }
add_action('init', 'my_plugin_register_cpt');

// REST endpoint
function my_plugin_rest_handler($request) { /* ... */ }
add_action('rest_api_init', function() {
    register_rest_route('my-plugin/v1', '/products', [/* ... */]);
});

// 40 more functions with no namespace, no class, no autoload
// untestable, undiscoverable, guaranteed to conflict with something
entries.test_step: Run `composer validate` inside the plugin directory — exits 0. Run `vendor/bin/phpunit` — tests pass. Grep for function definitions at the file level (outside a class) in src/: `grep -r "^function " src/` should return nothing. Every class should be in its own file matching the PSR-4 path.

entries.title: README.md as the non-negotiable developer entry point
entries.summary: README.md is the entry point for every developer, including future you. A professional WordPress project README documents: how to set up a local environment, what the conventions are for branch names, plugin locations, and theme slugs, and what the standard workflow is. The goal is onboarding in 30 minutes instead of three days. Without it, developers lose time reorienting themselves every time they return to the project.
entries.code_example:
# README.md template

## My Project

Short description.

## Prerequisites
- PHP 8.3
- Composer 2.x
- DDEV 1.x
- WP-CLI 2.x

## Local setup

git clone git@github.com:agency/my-project.git
cd my-project
cp .env.example .env          # fill DB_NAME, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD
composer install
ddev start
./bin/scaffold.sh my-project  # installs WP, activates theme + plugins

## Conventions
- Branch naming: feature/TICKET-short-description, fix/TICKET-short-description
- Plugin location: wp-content/plugins/ — all managed via Composer
- Theme slug: my-theme
- New CPTs: wp-content/plugins/my-plugin/src/PostTypes/

## Deployment
Pushes to main trigger the CI pipeline and deploy to staging automatically.
entries.bad_pattern:
# README.md — the bare minimum that wastes everyone's time
# My Project
# This is a WordPress project.

# Or: no README.md at all.
# Result: every developer spends hours figuring out DB credentials, which
# plugins to activate, and what the folder conventions are.
entries.test_step: Hand the README to a developer who has never seen the project. Time how long it takes them to have a working local environment. Target: under 30 minutes. Anything longer means the README is missing steps.

entries.title: Keep folder paths consistent across all projects in the agency
entries.summary: Folder paths should never vary between projects in the same team or agency. Do not switch between assets/js, js/, or static/js across projects. The first time a developer switches to a different project and has to relearn where everything lives, structure has failed its purpose. The system accelerates work; inconsistency negates that advantage immediately.
entries.code_example:
# Agency folder conventions — apply to every project

# Asset pipeline output (never edit directly):
assets/css/      # compiled stylesheets
assets/js/       # compiled JavaScript bundles

# Source code (edit these):
src/             # PHP classes, PSR-4 namespace root
src/PostTypes/
src/Api/
src/Helpers/

# Config (environment-specific, never committed):
config/          # server-side config files read at runtime
.env             # local overrides (in .gitignore)
.env.example     # template (committed)

# Scripts:
bin/             # scaffold.sh, deploy.sh, lint.sh

# Tests:
tests/           # PHPUnit test files mirroring src/ structure
entries.bad_pattern:
# Project A:
assets/js/
inc/classes/
scripts/

# Project B (same agency, same team):
static/js/
lib/
bin/

# Project C:
js/
classes/
tools/

# Result: three projects, three different folder conventions.
# Every developer switches context repeatedly and must re-learn
# where everything lives each time.
entries.test_step: Open three projects from your agency in separate terminal tabs. Run ls in each root. Can you immediately find assets, PHP classes, and setup scripts using the same folder names in all three? If not, document the standard and migrate the outliers.

entries.title: Git branching model — the five-branch structure that prevents deployment chaos
entries.summary: Without a defined branching structure, direct pushes to main and unnamed branches accumulate until a merge is a nightmare. The five-branch model that works across dozens of projects: main (never touched directly), staging (integration target, everything lands here before testing), feature/* (one task, fully isolated), hotfix/* (urgent fixes, clearly separated from feature work), release/* (launch preparation). Commits directly to main are forbidden without exception.
entries.code_example:
# Create and use the five-branch model

# Feature work
git checkout -b feature/TICKET-add-product-schema
# ... implement, commit, push
git push -u origin feature/TICKET-add-product-schema
# Open PR → staging, get review, merge

# Urgent fix
git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix/fix-payment-redirect
# ... fix, commit
git push -u origin hotfix/fix-payment-redirect
# Open PR → main + staging simultaneously

# Release preparation
git checkout -b release/1.4.0
# bump version, finalise changelog
git push -u origin release/1.4.0
# PR → main, tag after merge
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book explicitly calls out as wrong:

# 1. Direct push to main — forbidden without exception
git checkout main
git commit -m "fixed the thing"
git push origin main

# 2. No naming convention
git checkout -b "new-try-2"
git checkout -b "last-changes-final_final"

# 3. No staging branch — features go straight from feature/* to main
# without integration testing
entries.test_step: Run `git branch -a` and verify main, staging, and at least one feature/* branch exist. Confirm main has a branch protection rule (Settings → Branches → require PR before merging). Confirm no direct commits land on main: `git log --first-parent origin/main` should show only merge commits.

entries.title: Commit messages as micro-documentation — readable months later
entries.summary: Write commit messages so that you, or a teammate, can understand them months later without asking anyone. A commit is micro-documentation, not a puzzle. Conventional commit prefixes (feat:, fix:, refactor:) tell reviewers and CI what changed. Unhelpful messages ("update", "new try", "final version") make debugging, history review, and onboarding significantly slower — they are the Git equivalent of variable names like x and y.
entries.code_example:
# Helpful commit messages
git commit -m "feat: add 2FA to login process"
git commit -m "fix: prevent slider jump in Safari"
git commit -m "refactor: modularize theme asset loader"
git commit -m "chore: remove unused translation files"
git commit -m "docs: update onboarding README with DDEV steps"

# With a body when the why matters
git commit -m "fix: revert WP 6.7 block renderer to legacy path

Block renderer in 6.7 introduced a regression for dynamic blocks
that read query vars during init. Reverting to the 6.6 path until
upstream fix lands. Tracked in #142."
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book explicitly calls "not helpful"
git commit -m "update"
git commit -m "new try"
git commit -m "final version"
git commit -m "asdf"
git commit -m "changes"
git commit -m "WIP"

# These tell you nothing when you run git log six months later.
# You cannot search them, you cannot filter them in CI, and you
# cannot generate a meaningful changelog from them.
entries.test_step: Run `git log --oneline -30` on the main branch. Count how many messages start with a conventional prefix (feat:, fix:, chore:, refactor:, docs:). If fewer than 80% use a prefix, establish the convention in CONTRIBUTING.md and add a commit-msg hook to enforce it.

entries.title: .gitignore — source code in, generated folders and secrets out
entries.summary: You do not have to version everything — in fact, you should not. Build artifacts (dist/, node_modules/, vendor/), environment files (.env, .env.local), system caches, and temporary files have no place in Git. If you use Composer and npm, all you need in the repo are the definition files: composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json. `composer install` and `npm install` restore the rest deterministically. The code is what matters, not generated folders.
entries.code_example:
# .gitignore — professional WordPress project baseline

# Composer dependencies (run: composer install)
/vendor/

# npm/node (run: npm install)
/node_modules/

# Build output (run: npm run build)
/dist/
assets/*.min.css
assets/*.min.js

# WordPress core if managed by Composer
/wp/

# Environment files — NEVER commit these
.env
.env.local
.env.staging
.env.prod

# Template stays committed so new developers know what variables to fill
!.env.example

# OS/IDE noise
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
.idea/
.vscode/
entries.bad_pattern:
# What should NOT be in .gitignore:
#   composer.lock  — removing this breaks reproducible installs
#   composer.json  — this is your dependency manifest, it belongs in Git
#   package.json   — same reason
#   package-lock.json — same as composer.lock

# What should NOT be committed:
git add vendor/          # 50MB of Composer packages in history
git add node_modules/    # hundreds of MB, conflicts on every install
git add .env             # exposes database passwords and API keys
entries.test_step: Run `git status` after a fresh `composer install && npm install`. Confirm vendor/ and node_modules/ appear as ignored (not as untracked). Run `git ls-files | grep ".env$"` — should return nothing. Check `git ls-files composer.lock` — should return composer.lock.

entries.title: Semantic versioning + release-it — structured, automated releases
entries.summary: Every release needs a clear versioning standard. Semantic Versioning (SemVer) provides it: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — e.g. 2.3.1. MAJOR signals breaking changes, MINOR adds backwards-compatible features, PATCH delivers fixes with no side effects. Pre-releases like 1.0.0-beta.1 or 2.0.0-rc.2 are especially useful in CI-based preview deployments. release-it automates the whole cycle: version bump, tag, changelog generation, GitHub release, npm publish — one command, consistently reproducible.
entries.bad_pattern:
# Anti-patterns the book calls out:
# 1. No versioning at all — "we'll add it later"
# 2. Manual version bumps in multiple places (plugin header, package.json, style.css)
#    — they drift out of sync
# 3. Tags like "v1-final", "v2-working", "v3-BACKUP"
#    — not SemVer, breaks tooling that relies on semver parsing
# 4. Releasing directly from a local dev environment without a clean build
#    — local dev artifacts, unbuilt assets, and debug flags go live
entries.test_step: Run `git tag --sort=-version:refname | head -5` to see recent tags. Confirm they follow vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format. Run `npx release-it --dry-run` to confirm the release-it config is valid and the next version bump is as expected.

entries.title: Unified asset pipeline — Composer + npm in one project, never split
entries.summary: Most WordPress projects suffer from a split personality: PHP and Composer on one side, SCSS and npm/Vite on the other. If your PHP stack is neatly versioned while your frontend is FTP-uploaded fragments, your Composer workflow is meaningless. The fix is treating Composer and npm as one system: source files (SCSS, unminified JS) in version control, build artifacts (dist/app.min.css, dist/app.min.js) never committed, a single defined build command (npm run build), and the entire pipeline integrated into CI so broken or unbuilt assets never reach production.
entries.code_example:
# package.json — asset pipeline commands
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "dev": "vite",
    "lint": "eslint src/",
    "test": "vitest run"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "vite": "^5.0.0",
    "sass": "^1.70.0"
  }
}

# .gitignore — build output never in version control
/dist/
*.min.css
*.min.js

# CI step that ties both package managers together
- name: Install PHP deps
  run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist

- name: Install JS deps
  run: npm ci

- name: Build assets
  run: npm run build
entries.bad_pattern:
# The split personality — what the book explicitly calls chaos:

# 1. PHP stack versioned via Composer, frontend uploaded manually via FTP
# 2. node_modules/ committed to Git ("so everyone has the same version")
# 3. Compiled dist/ files committed to Git ("so the server doesn't need Node")
# 4. No npm run build step in CI — assets only build on a developer's laptop
# 5. Different build tool per developer (one uses Webpack, one uses Gulp)
#    — "it works on my machine" becomes the only truth
entries.test_step: On a fresh clone, run `composer install --no-dev && npm ci && npm run build`. Confirm the build succeeds and dist/ files appear. Confirm dist/ is not tracked by Git: `git ls-files dist/` must return nothing. Confirm node_modules/ is not tracked: `git ls-files node_modules/` must return nothing.

entries.title: Three-environment structure — local, staging, production with defined flags per stage
entries.summary: Most developers distinguish only between local and live and miss everything in between. A realistic setup needs three stages: local (debug on, only you), staging (real content, logging on, team and client), production (anything that could interfere: off, public). These environments must be anchored in the project via configs and WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE — not in your head. Since WordPress 5.5 the function wp_get_environment_type() returns one of local, development, staging, production and should be used consistently throughout the codebase to gate debug behaviour, mail delivery, and query logging.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// wp-config.php — reading environment type from .env / server variable
define('WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE', getenv('WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE') ?: 'production');

// Using wp_get_environment_type() to gate behaviour
if (wp_get_environment_type() === 'local') {
    define('WP_DEBUG',         true);
    define('WP_DEBUG_LOG',     true);
    define('SAVEQUERIES',      true);
    define('SCRIPT_DEBUG',     true);
} elseif (wp_get_environment_type() === 'staging') {
    define('WP_DEBUG',         true);
    define('WP_DEBUG_LOG',     true);
    define('SAVEQUERIES',      false);
    define('SCRIPT_DEBUG',     false);
} else {
    // production
    define('WP_DEBUG',         false);
    define('SAVEQUERIES',      false);
    define('SCRIPT_DEBUG',     false);
}

// Mail driver gate — prevent real emails from staging
if (wp_get_environment_type() !== 'production') {
    add_filter('wp_mail', function ($args) {
        // redirect all mail to null or a test inbox
        $args['to'] = 'dev-catch@example.com';
        return $args;
    });
}
entries.test_step: Run `wp eval "echo wp_get_environment_type();"` on each environment. Confirm it returns local on dev, staging on the staging server, production on the live server. Confirm WP_DEBUG is false on production: `wp eval "echo WP_DEBUG ? true : false;"` must print false on live.

entries.title: .env pattern — template committed, actual file gitignored, secrets injected per environment
entries.summary: .env files with API keys, passwords, and tokens still land on GitHub every day — usually with a commit message like "add env for staging (temp!)", and three commits later nobody deletes it. The correct pattern has five steps: create a .env.example with placeholders (committed), add .env to .gitignore, use per-environment variants (.env.local, .env.staging, .env.prod) stored locally or injected by CI, load them with a Dotenv library, and never hardcode plain text keys in code. You do not need an additional secrets tool — you need discipline.
entries.code_example:
# .env.example — committed, placeholders only
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_USER=root
DB_PASSWORD=changeme
WP_HOME=https://myproject.test
WP_SITEURL=https://myproject.test/wp
APP_SECRET=changeme
MAIL_DRIVER=log
WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE=local

# .gitignore additions
.env
.env.local
.env.staging
.env.prod
!.env.example

# GitHub Actions — correct secret reference
env:
  SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY_STAGING }}

# PHP — load the .env file with phpdotenv
require_once __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';
$dotenv = Dotenv\Dotenv::createImmutable(__DIR__);
$dotenv->load();
$dbHost = $_ENV['DB_HOST'];
entries.test_step: Run `git ls-files .env .env.local .env.staging .env.prod` — must return nothing. Run `git ls-files .env.example` — must return .env.example. On a fresh clone, copy .env.example to .env, fill the values, run `composer install`, and confirm the application loads without errors.

entries.title: Secrets management — isolation, secure storage, controlled usage, rotation
entries.summary: Secrets are digital keys. Whoever holds them has access — to databases, payment providers, internal APIs. An API key in plain text on GitHub can be picked up by bots within seconds. Good secrets management has three core tasks: isolation (each key belongs to exactly one environment with minimum rights), secure storage (never in plain-text repos — .env files outside the repo, or dedicated secret stores), and controlled usage (access granted only when needed, only by authorized processes, for exactly as long as needed). Add regular rotation and secret scanning, and the system stays closed even when the worst happens.
entries.code_example:
# GitHub Actions — secret injected in memory only during the build step
# Key is never stored in the repo, on the build server, or permanently on the target server.

- name: Deploy via SSH
  env:
    SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY_PROD }}
  run: |
    echo "$SSH_KEY" | ssh-add -
    rsync -avz --exclude='.env' dist/ user@production.example.com:/var/www/html/

# The SSH key exists only in memory during this step.
# After execution it is discarded — not written to disk, not logged.

# Naming convention from the book — clear, environment-scoped, no abbreviations:
# DEPLOY_KEY_STAGING
# DEPLOY_KEY_PROD
# MAILGUN_TOKEN
# APP_SECRET
# SLACK_WEBHOOK_STAGING
entries.bad_pattern:
# Bad practices table from the book:

# Storage: API key hardcoded in wp-config.php in repo
define('MAILGUN_API_KEY', 'key-abc123secret'); // committed to Git

# Distribution: secret shared via Slack or email
# → not auditable, not revokable, might be screenshotted

# Access: every developer has full production access
# → one compromised account = full breach

# Rotation: never
# → keys from 2019 still active in 2026

# Environment split: same key everywhere
define('APP_SECRET', 'shared-secret'); // on local, staging, AND production

# Logging: secrets written to error log
error_log('Using secret: ' . $secret); // exposed in log files
entries.test_step: Enable GitHub secret scanning on the repository (Settings → Security → Secret scanning). Run Gitleaks on the history: `docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/path ghcr.io/gitleaks/gitleaks:latest detect --source /path`. Audit every GitHub secret: confirm each has a clear name, an owning environment scope, and a known rotation date.

entries.title: Release models for themes and plugins — public, private, hybrid, SaaS, marketplace
entries.summary: Before the first build, decide how you will distribute your theme or plugin — that choice defines testing, infrastructure, support, and rollout. Five models exist: public (WordPress.org/GitHub, wide reach, no license protection), private (your own server, license checks, full control but more overhead), hybrid/freemium (free base + paid features, double housekeeping), SaaS (Freemius/Lemon Squeezy/Paddle, fast start but vendor dependency and fees), marketplace (Envato/ThemeForest, platform handles checkout, strict rules). Each has trade-offs — choose deliberately, not by default.
entries.code_example:
# Practical tips for private releases (from the book):

# 1. Allow at least one staging domain per license
#    so updates can be tested safely before production.

# 2. Keep API logs to detect misuse (e.g., key sharing).

# 3. Serve ZIPs via time-limited tokens, not direct links:
#    /download?token=abc123&expires=1735000000&sig=HMAC_SHA256
#    The token is valid only for a short window.

# 4. Always keep a stable previous version ready for quick rollback.

# Hybrid release — separate update channels:
# Free:  update endpoint = https://updates.example.com/free/my-plugin
# Pro:   update endpoint = https://updates.example.com/pro/my-plugin
#        Pro endpoint requires a valid license key in the Authorization header.
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book documents as failure patterns:

# 1. Zipping a release from a local dev environment
#    — unbuilt assets, debug flags, dev-only files go live

# 2. No staging tests before release
#    — fatal errors and white-screen errors appear after customers update

# 3. No rollback version available
#    — a bad release can only be fixed forward, not rolled back

# 4. One update endpoint for both free and Pro
#    — Pro features leak to free users or free users get Pro update prompts

# 5. Starting with SaaS and never planning an exit
#    — customer data flows through the vendor; migration later is painful
entries.test_step: If using a private release model: confirm ZIPs are served via time-limited signed tokens, not permanent direct links. Confirm a staging domain per license is allowed. Test a rollback: pull the previous ZIP from the update server and install it via WP-CLI — confirm it installs cleanly without errors.

entries.title: Update server + CI/CD release workflow — six steps from merge to customer update
entries.summary: A professional release is not a lucky byproduct of weeks of coding — it is a planned, tested, documented routine. The six-step workflow the book defines: (1) finalise the code and run checks (PHPStan, WP Coding Standards), (2) bump the version via CI or style.css/plugin header (never manually in multiple places), (3) generate the changelog from pull request labels into Markdown per release, (4) build the ZIP on a build server removing dev dependencies, (5) upload to the update server with release.json and license checks, (6) roll out to staging first, then live, watching logs and support closely.
entries.code_example:
# Minimal GitHub Actions release workflow (excerpt)
# .github/workflows/release.yml

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*.*.*'

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist && npm ci

      - name: Build assets
        run: npm run build

      - name: Bump version in plugin header
        run: |
          VERSION=${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/v}
          sed -i "s/^ \* Version: .*/ * Version: ${VERSION}/" my-plugin.php

      - name: Build ZIP (no dev files)
        run: |
          zip -r my-plugin-${VERSION}.zip . \
            --exclude="*.git*" --exclude="node_modules/*" \
            --exclude="tests/*" --exclude=".env*"

      - name: Generate changelog from PR labels
        uses: mikepenz/release-changelog-builder-action@v4
        with:
          configuration: .github/changelog-config.json

      - name: Upload to update server
        run: |
          curl -X POST https://updates.example.com/upload \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.UPDATE_SERVER_TOKEN }}" \
            -F "file=@my-plugin-${VERSION}.zip" \
            -F "version=${VERSION}"
entries.bad_pattern:
# Common failure patterns from the book:

# 1. Changelog is empty
#    — labels don't match the config. Fix: ensure label names exactly match changelog-config.json.

# 2. Wrong version in the package
#    — version set manually in multiple places and they drifted.
#    Fix: always pull the version directly from the Git tag.

# 3. 404 on the changelog in the WP info dialog
#    — Markdown file stored in the wrong path.
#    Fix: correct the path in the release workflow.

# 4. Info dialog is empty in wp-admin
#    — plugins_api() / themes_api() filter not implemented.
#    Fix: add the hook implementation that fetches the changelog URL.

# 5. Build happens on a developer's laptop, not on CI
#    — local dev artifacts, debug flags, and node_modules residue go into the ZIP.
entries.test_step: Push a tag (e.g. v1.5.0) to the repository. Confirm the release workflow runs and produces a ZIP without node_modules/, vendor/ dev packages, or .env files. Confirm the release.json on the update server reflects the new version. Install the ZIP on a staging site via WP-CLI: `wp plugin install https://updates.example.com/download/my-plugin-1.5.0.zip --activate` — must succeed.

entries.title: Monorepo vs. multirepo — the conscious decision that prevents Git chaos
entries.summary: Most projects start as one repo and expand without a conscious decision. After a year there are ten repos, nobody can say where specific code belongs, and half a day is lost each week keeping setups aligned. The two primary structures: monorepo (all code in one repo — themes, plugins, MU-plugins, config; fast onboarding, simple CI, but coarse releases and limited permissions) or multirepo (each component in its own repo — granular releases, reusability, but more pipelines and coordination). The rule of thumb: start lean with monorepo while the team is small, adopt Composer and a private registry from day one, so the shift to multirepo later is a clean transition without chaos.
entries.code_example:
# Monorepo structure — typical agency project
my-wp-project/                # one repo for the whole site
├── mu-plugins/
│   └── project-core/
├── plugins/
│   ├── my-events/
│   └── my-shop/
├── themes/
│   └── my-theme/
├── config/
├── tests/
└── composer.json             # one lockfile governs everything

# Multirepo structure — agency with reusable packages
agency/project-core      → git@github.com:agency/project-core.git
agency/my-events-plugin  → git@github.com:agency/my-events-plugin.git
agency/my-theme          → git@github.com:agency/my-theme.git

# project-specific repo pulls them all in via Composer
{
  "require": {
    "agency/project-core": "^2.1",
    "agency/my-events-plugin": "^1.5",
    "agency/my-theme": "^3.0"
  },
  "repositories": [
    { "type": "composer", "url": "https://packages.agency.example.com" }
  ]
}
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book describes as the chaos state:
# - 10 developers, 8 repositories, 5 CI workflows
# - No shared standards between repos
# - Each repo has its own folder conventions, commit styles, and CI config
# - Every week, half a day lost just keeping setups aligned
# - Onboarding takes 2 full days instead of a few hours

# Also wrong: using Git submodules as the distribution mechanism
# Submodules appear tidy but in practice lead to:
#   - missed updates (submodule pointer left at old commit)
#   - merge conflicts on submodule references
#   - confusion about detached HEAD states
# The book's verdict: "Submodules cause errors. ZIP files are stopgaps.
# A private registry is the only professional solution."
entries.test_step: If on monorepo: run `git log --oneline -20` on main — confirm all component work appears in one history, easy to read. If on multirepo: run `composer show` in the project root — confirm each internal package resolves to the expected version from the private registry, not from a local path or submodule.

entries.title: Private Composer registry with Satis — distributing internal packages professionally
entries.summary: Whether monorepo or multirepo, custom code must be distributed reliably. ZIP files spread through Slack channels and email threads until nobody knows which version is current. Submodules are fragile in practice. The professional answer is Composer with a private registry: Satis (open source, self-hosted, flexible — best for teams that want control) or Private Packagist (SaaS, ready to use — best for teams that want convenience). Internal packages install exactly like external ones. Five-step setup: choose a registry, register Git repos as packages, configure CI to publish releases automatically, point composer.json to the registry, review and archive outdated packages.
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book replaces with a private registry:

# 1. ZIP files via Slack / Google Drive / email
#    "Here's the latest my-plugin-v2-final-FINAL.zip"
#    — no version tracking, wrong person gets the wrong file

# 2. Git submodules
git submodule add git@github.com:agency/project-core.git wp-content/mu-plugins/project-core
#    — fragile, missed updates, detached HEAD confusion, painful on CI

# 3. Composer type:path in production
{
  "repositories": [
    { "type": "path", "url": "../project-core" }
  ]
}
#    — works only if the sibling directory exists on the server (it never does in CI)

# The book's verdict: "Submodules cause errors. ZIP files are stopgaps.
# A private registry is the only professional solution."
entries.test_step: Run `php bin/satis build satis.json public/` and confirm the output directory contains packages.json. Point a test project at the registry, run `composer require agency/my-plugin`, and confirm it installs from your registry (not from GitHub directly). Run `composer show agency/my-plugin` to verify the installed version matches the tag you pushed.

entries.title: Testing in WordPress — the right tests, not all of them
entries.summary: Most WordPress projects have no test setup. Not because it is too complicated, but because nobody feels responsible. "WordPress is a CMS, not a framework." "The client tests during approval anyway." These attitudes push bugs into production. You do not need 100 tests or full coverage — you need the tests that stop you when something important breaks. Not academic. Just a safeguard: if this check fails, I do not want to deploy.
entries.code_example:
# The five questions to start with — each maps to one test

# 1. Is the contact form reachable and submittable?
#    → Playwright E2E: navigate to /contact, fill, click submit, assert thank-you page

# 2. Does the shortcode render?
#    → PHPUnit: apply_filters('the_content', '[download-button]'), assertStringContains('<a')

# 3. Does is_user_logged_in() behave correctly?
#    → PHPUnit: wp_set_current_user(0), assertFalse(is_user_logged_in())
#               wp_set_current_user(1), assertTrue(is_user_logged_in())

# 4. Does the REST API return valid JSON?
#    → PHPUnit: dispatch a WP_REST_Request, json_decode the body, assertNotNull

# 5. Can a post be saved with special characters?
#    → PHPUnit: wp_insert_post(['post_title' => 'Test & "Quote" <Tag>']),
#               assertGreaterThan(0, $post_id)
entries.bad_pattern:
# Testing anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. "The client tests on staging" — not automated, not reproducible
# 2. No test directory in the repo at all
# 3. Manual clicking before every deploy — not scalable, misses regressions
# 4. Writing tests only for edge cases and not the critical happy path
#    (contact form, checkout, login) — the happy path is where real damage happens
entries.test_step: Open the project root. Is there a tests/ directory with at least one file? Is there a phpunit.xml.dist? Is there a CI step that runs the test suite? If any answer is no — the project is one silent failure away from a client incident.

entries.title: PHPUnit setup in a WordPress project — lean, usable, effective
entries.summary: PHPUnit is still the standard for WordPress unit and integration testing. You do not need a test database, a Selenium server, or a CI monster. You need a setup light enough to actually use and strong enough to protect you. Start with `composer require --dev phpunit/phpunit` and a phpunit.xml.dist file. Optionally add `brain/monkey` for mocking WordPress functions without bootstrapping WP. A good test checks exactly one thing — and that one thing can decide whether a deployment succeeds or fails.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// tests/Shortcodes/DownloadButtonTest.php
// Tests the [download-button] shortcode that renders an anchor tag.

namespace MyPlugin\Tests\Shortcodes;

use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

class DownloadButtonTest extends TestCase
{
    public function test_renders_anchor_with_href(): void
    {
        // Call the shortcode handler directly (no WP bootstrap needed).
        $output = render_download_button_shortcode([
            'url'   => 'https://example.com/file.zip',
            'label' => 'Download',
        ]);

        $this->assertStringContainsString('<a', $output);
        $this->assertStringContainsString('https://example.com/file.zip', $output);
        $this->assertStringContainsString('Download', $output);
    }

    public function test_renders_nothing_without_url(): void
    {
        $output = render_download_button_shortcode([]);
        $this->assertEmpty($output);
    }
}
entries.bad_pattern:
# PHPUnit anti-patterns in WordPress projects:

# 1. No phpunit.xml.dist — every developer runs the suite differently
#    or with different configuration:
#    vendor/bin/phpunit --bootstrap tests/bootstrap.php tests/
#    vendor/bin/phpunit -c my-custom-config.xml
#    → nobody agrees on what "the test suite" means

# 2. Tests that bootstrap the full WordPress environment when only a helper
#    function is being tested — slow, fragile, unnecessary:
#    require_once ABSPATH . 'wp-load.php'; // 500ms startup just to test a string helper

# 3. A single monolithic test file with 30 test methods for unrelated features
#    — one failure blocks the entire run and the output is unreadable
entries.test_step: Run `vendor/bin/phpunit --version` to confirm PHPUnit is installed. Run `vendor/bin/phpunit` from the project root — the suite must start and complete (pass or fail, not error on config). Add at least one test for the most critical business logic in the project (price calculation, access check, or REST response shape).

entries.title: WP-CLI scaffold test — generate PHPUnit boilerplate for plugins and themes
entries.summary: WP-CLI includes a scaffold command that generates the PHPUnit boilerplate for a plugin or theme: phpunit.xml, bootstrap.php, a sample test, and the install-wp-tests.sh script that sets up a local WordPress test database. This is the fastest way to get from zero to a running PHPUnit suite inside a WordPress project.
entries.code_example:
# Generate PHPUnit scaffold for a plugin
wp scaffold plugin-tests my-plugin

# This creates:
# tests/
#   bootstrap.php
#   test-sample.php
# phpunit.xml.dist
# bin/
#   install-wp-tests.sh

# Run the install script (one-time setup per environment):
bash bin/install-wp-tests.sh wordpress_test root '' localhost latest

# Run the suite
vendor/bin/phpunit
entries.bad_pattern:
# Manual PHP test setup anti-patterns:

# 1. Hand-rolling bootstrap.php from scratch:
#    require_once dirname( dirname( __FILE__ ) ) . '/wp-load.php';
#    ... 40 lines of path juggling ...
#    Use wp scaffold plugin-tests instead — it generates the correct bootstrap.

# 2. Committing the generated test DB config to Git:
#    wp-tests-config.php contains DB credentials — add it to .gitignore.
#    The scaffold install script generates it on each machine from parameters.

# 3. Running tests against the real production DB
#    — the test suite uses transactions and TRUNCATES tables.
#    Always use a separate test database.
entries.test_step: Run `wp scaffold plugin-tests --help` to confirm WP-CLI supports the command. After scaffolding, confirm `bin/install-wp-tests.sh` exists and runs without errors on a clean environment. Run `vendor/bin/phpunit` and confirm the sample test passes.

entries.title: Playwright E2E setup — real clicks, real forms, CI-ready in under five minutes
entries.summary: Unit tests pass but the login button is set to display:none in CSS. Or a JS update blocked the submit event. Or wp-login.php redirects to a maintenance page. Nobody catches these until the customer complains. Playwright simulates real clicks, keyboard actions, and form submissions — the same workflow a human would use. One `npm init playwright@latest` generates a working test setup with no extra packages and no cloud service. Five to eight E2E tests per project are enough to cover critical flows.
entries.bad_pattern:
# Playwright anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Testing with the login button hidden by CSS — nobody notices until a client
#    complains. E2E tests catch this; unit tests do not.

# 2. Running Playwright only before a major release, not on every PR:
#    → regressions accumulate undetected across many commits

# 3. Writing 30 Playwright tests when 5 well-chosen ones cover the same risk:
#    → maintenance burden rises, tests become flaky, the team skips them
#    → five focused tests that run reliably beat thirty that nobody trusts

# 4. Not running E2E in CI at all:
#    → "green unit tests" does not mean "the login works"
entries.test_step: Run `npx playwright --version` to confirm installation. Run `npx playwright test` — the suite must start without errors. Confirm at least one test navigates to and clicks an interactive element (form, login, menu). Add a nightly schedule in CI that runs the full E2E suite against the staging URL.

entries.title: Playwright in GitHub Actions — two run modes for PRs and nightly checks
entries.summary: E2E tests are only valuable when they run automatically. Two Playwright run modes in GitHub Actions: on every pull request to catch obvious breakage before merging, and nightly via schedule to verify external services are still available. Saving failed screenshots as CI artifacts gives the team visual context when a test fails — debugging without screenshots is like searching blindfolded.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — Playwright in CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, staging]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'   # nightly at 02:00 UTC

jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps

      - name: Run E2E tests
        run: npx playwright test

      - name: Upload failed screenshots
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: visual-diffs
          path: test-results/
entries.bad_pattern:
# CI anti-patterns the book calls out:

# 1. Running E2E tests only manually before a release:
#    → by the time someone runs them, regressions are weeks old

# 2. A single 'composer ci' command that runs PHPUnit, Playwright, linting,
#    and three bash scripts all at once:
#    → when it fails, nobody knows if the failure is code, a snapshot, or the linter
#    → separate each test type into its own named CI step

# 3. No artifact upload on failure:
#    → debugging a failing Playwright test without screenshots means re-running
#    → a screenshot often shows the bug in 10 seconds; log-reading takes hours

# 4. Running E2E against a production URL without an approval gate:
#    → can trigger real transactions, emails, and side effects
entries.test_step: Check the GitHub Actions workflow for a Playwright step. Confirm it uses `npx playwright install --with-deps` before running tests. Confirm failed tests upload artifacts: look for `actions/upload-artifact` in the workflow. Confirm at least one test run mode is tied to pull_request and one to a schedule.

entries.title: Visual regression testing with Playwright — pixel diff before the client sees it
entries.summary: Your code is fine. Your tests are green. But a plugin update shifted a button — the CTA disappeared on mobile and nobody noticed until the client sent a screenshot. Playwright supports screenshot-based visual regression: on the first run it creates a reference screenshot; from the second run onward it compares pixel by pixel. Use a tolerance (threshold) to avoid false positives from sub-pixel rendering differences. Store screenshot diffs as CI artifacts so the team can see what changed directly in the pull request.
entries.bad_pattern:
# Visual regression anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. No visual tests at all — layout bugs like a disappeared CTA are invisible
#    until a client sends a screenshot.

# 2. Auto-failing CI on every visual diff (even a 0.5px shadow):
#    → team stops touching CSS to avoid triggering diffs
#    → result: stagnation instead of control

# 3. Not setting a threshold:
#    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('page.png');
#    → sub-pixel rendering differences between OS/browser versions cause
#    → constant failures that have nothing to do with real regressions

# 4. Not masking dynamic content before diffing:
#    → timestamps, countdown timers, rotating banners change on every run
#    → screenshots never match the reference

# 5. Using different fonts locally vs. in CI:
#    → font rendering differences cause constant "diffs" in text-heavy pages
entries.test_step: Run `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` once to create reference screenshots. Run `npx playwright test` a second time — all visual tests must pass with the existing references. Confirm screenshot files are committed to tests/screenshots/ (or the configured directory). Confirm the workflow uploads `test-results/` as an artifact on failure so diffs are visible in the PR.

entries.title: Test data with Faker — realistic, reproducible, never relying on manual content
entries.summary: Tests that rely on existing content are not automated — they are lucky. Post #42, a contact form with ID 7, a product named "Test Product" — and then a colleague deletes the page. Everything fails without a single line of code changing. The fix: generate all test data programmatically before each test run using fakerphp/faker. Faker creates realistic names, emails, prices, and body text in seconds. Combined with wp_insert_post() and WP-CLI, you can build any state you need — clean, predictable, repeatable — without touching the WP admin.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// tests/Support/DataFactory.php
// Factory that creates realistic WP test data using fakerphp/faker.

namespace MyPlugin\Tests\Support;

use Faker\Factory;

class DataFactory
{
    private \Faker\Generator $faker;

    public function __construct()
    {
        $this->faker = Factory::create();
    }

    /**
     * Create a published post with realistic content and return its ID.
     */
    public function createPost(array $overrides = []): int
    {
        $defaults = [
            'post_title'   => $this->faker->sentence(5),
            'post_content' => $this->faker->paragraphs(3, true),
            'post_status'  => 'publish',
            'post_type'    => 'post',
        ];

        $id = wp_insert_post(array_merge($defaults, $overrides));
        if (is_wp_error($id)) {
            throw new \RuntimeException('wp_insert_post failed: ' . $id->get_error_message());
        }

        return $id;
    }

    /**
     * Create a dummy user with a safe @example.com address.
     */
    public function createUser(string $role = 'subscriber'): int
    {
        return wp_create_user(
            $this->faker->userName(),
            wp_generate_password(),
            // Never use a real domain — .example.com addresses never deliver mail.
            $this->faker->userName() . '@example.com'
        );
    }
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// Anti-patterns the book documents:

// 1. Test that relies on a hardcoded post ID
$post = get_post(42);  // ID 42 exists locally, but not on staging or CI
$this->assertNotNull($post);  // fails randomly

// 2. Tests on real product names from a DB dump
$product = wc_get_product(get_page_by_path('my-test-product', OBJECT, 'product'));
// slug exists on one machine, someone deleted it on staging last week

// 3. Real email address in a dummy user — CI run sends a notification
wp_create_user('testuser', 'pass', 'jane.smith@clientdomain.com');
// CI ran a "send confirmation" hook and emailed the real person

// 4. Assuming test DB has content from production
$count = $wpdb->get_var("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {$wpdb->posts}");
$this->assertGreaterThan(0, $count);  // passes locally, fails on fresh CI DB
entries.test_step: Run `composer show fakerphp/faker` — it must appear in dev dependencies. Confirm there is a factory class or seeder script in tests/Support/ or tests/Factories/. Run a test that calls the factory and verify the test passes on a fresh, empty DB (wipe and rerun to confirm it does not depend on pre-existing content).

entries.title: WP-CLI seeding scripts — reproducible test data in one command
entries.summary: WP-CLI goes beyond plugin management. You can write seeder scripts that create posts, pages, users, products, and options in a single command. In CI nothing runs by hand — data must be created during setup, clean and predictable, with a single command. Locally you might want 30–50 posts; in CI five are enough to check if loops work. Control the count via a bash parameter or an ENV flag so the same script works in both contexts.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/seed-test-data.sh — one command to build a predictable WP state for tests

set -euo pipefail

POST_COUNT=${1:-5}
PRODUCT_COUNT=${2:-3}

# Posts
for i in $(seq 1 "$POST_COUNT"); do
  wp post create \
    --post_type=post \
    --post_status=publish \
    --post_title="Seed Post $i" \
    --allow-root
done

# WooCommerce products (if WooCommerce is active)
if wp plugin is-active woocommerce 2>/dev/null; then
  for i in $(seq 1 "$PRODUCT_COUNT"); do
    PRODUCT_ID=$(wp post create \
      --post_type=product \
      --post_status=publish \
      --post_title="Test Product $i" \
      --allow-root \
      --porcelain)
    # Set a defined price — never rely on "whatever was in the dump"
    wp post meta set "$PRODUCT_ID" _price "$(( i * 10 )).00" --allow-root
    wp post meta set "$PRODUCT_ID" _regular_price "$(( i * 10 )).00" --allow-root
  done
fi

echo "Seeded: $POST_COUNT posts, $PRODUCT_COUNT products."
entries.bad_pattern:
# WP-CLI seeding anti-patterns:

# 1. Importing a production DB dump and running tests against it:
#    → IDs shift on each import
#    → real customer emails can trigger notifications from test hooks
#    → nobody knows what "state" the dump represents

# 2. Creating test users with real email addresses:
#    wp user create tester jane.smith@realdomain.com --role=editor
#    → CI hooks that send "welcome" emails reach real inboxes

# 3. Tests that assume a post or user created in a previous test run still exists:
#    → the CI runner starts fresh; local dev may not
#    → every test or test file must set up and tear down its own data

# 4. Hardcoded post counts:
#    for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do wp post create ...; done
#    → use a variable so local dev can seed more without editing the script
entries.test_step: Run `wp --info` to confirm WP-CLI is available. Run `bash bin/seed-test-data.sh 3` on a clean WP install and confirm the command exits 0 and creates the expected posts. Run the same command twice and confirm it does not duplicate content (or that a reset step precedes it). Run `vendor/bin/phpunit` after seeding and confirm tests pass.

entries.title: PHPUnit factory methods — control your test data, control your tests
entries.summary: Write factory methods for every type of content you use repeatedly in tests. A factory method creates exactly what it says: a user, a product, a CPT with specific meta — in a defined state. You can use the WP_UnitTestCase factory (available when the WordPress test library is loaded) or write your own factory class. Either way, tests must never rely on content that already exists in the database. If your test depends on something a colleague can delete, you do not have a test — you have a house of cards.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// tests/PostTypes/EventPostTypeTest.php
// Uses the WP_UnitTestCase factory and a custom helper.

namespace MyPlugin\Tests\PostTypes;

use WP_UnitTestCase;

class EventPostTypeTest extends WP_UnitTestCase
{
    /**
     * Factory helper: create an event with required meta.
     */
    private function createEvent(array $overrides = []): int
    {
        $id = $this->factory->post->create(array_merge([
            'post_type'   => 'event',
            'post_status' => 'publish',
            'post_title'  => 'Test Event',
        ], $overrides));

        update_post_meta($id, '_event_date', '2026-09-01');
        update_post_meta($id, '_event_capacity', 50);

        return $id;
    }

    public function test_event_has_correct_capacity(): void
    {
        $id = $this->createEvent();
        $this->assertEquals('50', get_post_meta($id, '_event_capacity', true));
    }

    public function test_event_query_returns_only_events(): void
    {
        $this->createEvent(['post_title' => 'Event A']);
        $this->createEvent(['post_title' => 'Event B']);
        $this->factory->post->create(['post_type' => 'post']);

        $query = new \WP_Query(['post_type' => 'event', 'posts_per_page' => -1]);
        $this->assertEquals(2, $query->found_posts);
    }
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// Anti-patterns in WP unit tests — relying on pre-existing data

class BadEventTest extends WP_UnitTestCase
{
    public function test_event_has_capacity(): void
    {
        // WRONG: assumes post ID 42 exists and has the right meta
        $capacity = get_post_meta(42, '_event_capacity', true);
        $this->assertEquals('50', $capacity);
        // Fails on every fresh DB, CI runner, and staging server
    }

    public function test_event_list_is_not_empty(): void
    {
        // WRONG: relies on content from a DB import or manual setup
        $query = new \WP_Query(['post_type' => 'event']);
        $this->assertGreaterThan(0, $query->found_posts);
        // Passes locally, fails in CI where the DB is empty
    }
}
entries.test_step: Run the test suite on a fresh, empty WordPress database (reset with `wp db reset --yes`, reinstall core, then run `vendor/bin/phpunit`). All tests must pass without any manually created content. If any test fails on an empty DB but passes with existing data — it depends on manual content and the factory pattern must be applied.

entries.title: Composer scripts as the CI hinge — one entry point for every test type
