entries.summary: You should not have to guess whether it is `phpunit`, `vendor/bin/phpunit`, `./tests/run.sh`, or `make test`. There must be one Composer command. Define a clear set of scripts in composer.json so the team has one central entry point, CI and local environments behave identically, and nobody has excuses for not running tests. Every test type gets its own script — not a single `composer ci` that mixes everything into an unreadable blob.
entries.bad_pattern:
# What the book explicitly calls out as "no longer tolerated":

# 1. Tests that only run on one developer's machine:
#    "It works on my machine with my special database"
#    → not reproducible, not trustworthy

# 2. Hardcoded paths in shell scripts:
#    /Users/jan/Sites/project/vendor/bin/phpunit  # breaks on every other machine

# 3. A single 'composer ci' that mixes everything:
#    "composer ci" → PHPUnit + Playwright + linting + 3 bash scripts
#    → when it goes red, nobody knows which part failed
#    → separate each test type into its own named step

# 4. Comments like "# this is a CI dummy test":
#    → if the test is not real, delete it
#    → fake tests give false confidence and train the team to ignore failures
entries.test_step: Run `composer run-script --list` and confirm at least `test` and `lint` appear. Run `composer test` and confirm it starts PHPUnit without guessing the binary path. Add `composer test` to the CI workflow and confirm it is a separate, named step — not bundled with E2E or linting.

entries.title: PHP matrix builds — test against the PHP versions your clients actually run
entries.summary: If your project runs on shared hosting, you need to test against multiple PHP versions. Hosting reality is rarely bleeding edge. A plugin ran fine on PHP 8.2 — but on a client's 7.4 server, str_contains() blew up. That could have been avoided. GitHub Actions matrix strategy lets you run the same test suite against PHP 8.0, 8.1, and 8.2 in parallel, so PHP version regressions appear in CI before they appear on a client's server.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/tests.yml — PHP matrix builds

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, staging]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        php: ['8.0', '8.1', '8.2']

    name: "PHP ${{ matrix.php }}"

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up PHP
        uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: ${{ matrix.php }}
          extensions: pdo, pdo_mysql, mbstring
          coverage: none

      - name: Install Composer dependencies
        run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress

      - name: Run tests
        run: composer test
entries.bad_pattern:
# Matrix build anti-patterns:

# 1. Testing only against the latest PHP (8.2) when clients run 7.4 or 8.0:
#    → str_contains(), match expressions, named arguments: all PHP 8.0+
#    → $this->factory->post->create(): fine on 8.x, needs testing on 8.0

# 2. Using a PHP 8.1 function without checking minimum requirements:
#    $result = match ($status) {
#        'active'   => true,
#        'inactive' => false,
#    };
#    // Works on 8.0+, syntax error on 7.4 — only caught if you test against 7.4

# 3. Running the full matrix on every commit (including draft PRs):
#    → three parallel PHP builds on every WIP commit slows feedback
#    → restrict the full matrix to PRs targeting main/staging and merges to main
entries.test_step: Inspect the GitHub Actions workflow file. Confirm a `strategy: matrix: php:` block is present with at least two PHP versions. Run the workflow and confirm each matrix leg appears as a separate named check in the PR. If a function like `str_contains()` is used anywhere in the codebase, confirm it is tested against PHP 8.0 (where it was introduced) and that the composer.json `require.php` constraint matches.

entries.title: CI artifact collection — screenshots and logs when tests fail
entries.summary: When a test fails in CI, you need context. A Playwright screenshot caught a Safari-only layout bug that would have taken hours to reproduce locally. Debugging without images is like searching blindfolded. Configure every Playwright test to generate screenshots and logs on failure, save them as CI artifacts, and you can see what went wrong directly in the pull request — without re-running the suite locally.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml — artifact upload on failure

- name: Run E2E tests
  run: npx playwright test

- name: Upload failed screenshots
  if: failure()
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
  with:
    name: playwright-diffs
    path: test-results/

- name: Upload Playwright traces
  if: failure()
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
  with:
    name: playwright-traces
    path: playwright-report/

# Approval gate for production-like test environments
# Prevents CI from running against live APIs, real checkouts, or real email.

jobs:
  e2e-staging:
    environment:
      name: staging
      url: https://staging.example.com
    # No protection_rules needed for staging — runs automatically.

  e2e-production-like:
    environment:
      name: production-smoke
      protection_rules:
        required_reviewers:
          - lead-dev
    # This job only runs after a human clicks "Approve" in the GitHub UI.
entries.bad_pattern:
# CI debugging anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. No artifact upload on failure:
#    → when the test fails at 02:00, you re-run it at 09:00 with no idea what changed
#    → a screenshot would have shown the issue in 10 seconds

# 2. Running production-like E2E (checkout, booking, payment) without approval:
#    → CI accidentally bought real theater tickets during a test run
#    → gate production-like flows behind required_reviewers

# 3. Lumping all failure output into one undifferentiated artifact:
#    → 500MB zip of every log file, unnavigable
#    → upload focused artifacts: screenshots to 'playwright-diffs',
#       traces to 'playwright-traces', PHP logs to 'php-error-log'

# 4. Failing CI on every visual diff (even 0.5px shadow changes):
#    → team stops touching CSS
#    → save diffs as an artifact and let a human decide
entries.test_step: Trigger a deliberate Playwright test failure (e.g. assert a wrong page title). Confirm the workflow uploads a `playwright-diffs` artifact. Download the artifact and verify it contains a screenshot showing the failed state. Confirm any job that could trigger real external transactions is behind an `environment.protection_rules.required_reviewers` gate.

entries.title: CI pipeline stages for WordPress — install, lint, test, build, deploy in sequence
entries.summary: CI means every commit is checked automatically — no manual trigger required. Worst bugs are the ones that creep in quietly; CI catches them before they go live. The pipeline rests on three building blocks: jobs (individual tasks like composer install, phpunit, phpcs), stages (ordered groups: install → lint → test → build → deploy), and caching (~/.composer/cache, ~/.npm keyed to lock files). A working cache saves minutes per build, hours over time. The deploy stage only runs if all previous stages are green.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — staged WordPress CI pipeline

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, staging]
  push:
    branches: [main, staging]

jobs:
  install:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: '8.2'
          coverage: none
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.composer/cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-composer-${{ hashFiles('composer.lock') }}
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress

  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: install
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.2' }
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress
      - run: composer lint

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: install
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.2' }
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress
      - run: composer test

  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, test]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress
      - run: vendor/bin/dep deploy production
entries.bad_pattern:
# CI anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. One monolithic "do everything" job:
#    install && lint && test && build && deploy
#    → when it fails, nobody knows which part broke

# 2. No caching at all:
#    → downloads all Composer/npm deps on every run
#    → adds minutes per build, hours per week

# 3. Deploy runs even when tests fail:
#    no needs: [test] → broken code goes live

# 4. Build step inside the deploy job:
#    → a timeout during npm run build leaves the server half-deployed
#    → build must be its own named job, finished before deploy starts

# 5. No pipeline at all — "I test on my machine before pushing"
#    → wrong encoding, broken styles, a messed-up URL that only shows on staging
entries.test_step: Open .github/workflows/ (or .gitlab-ci.yml). Confirm the pipeline has at least three named stages: one that installs deps, one that runs linting or tests, and one that deploys only when the others succeed. Confirm Composer and npm caches are keyed to lock files. Trigger a deliberate test failure and confirm the deploy stage does not run.

entries.title: GitHub Actions vs. GitLab CI — which fits your WordPress project
entries.summary: Both GitHub Actions and GitLab CI give you free (or fair) CI resources without owning a server. GitHub Actions: very easy onboarding, strong templates, massive community, config in .github/workflows/*.yml. GitLab CI: more complex but highly flexible, built-in project management integration, config in .gitlab-ci.yml. The only thing that matters is to pick one and use it properly. If you are on GitHub, stick with Actions — the integration is seamless. If you work internally with GitLab, use its built-in CI for full control from issues to deployments. Deployment must always be controlled from the repository itself — no extra clicks, no UI hacks.
entries.code_example:
# GitHub Actions: deployments only from specific branches
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, 'release/*']

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # SSH key stored as a GitHub Secret — never hardcoded.
      - name: Deploy via Deployer
        env:
          SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
          DEPLOY_HOST: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }}
        run: |
          echo "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > /tmp/deploy_key
          chmod 600 /tmp/deploy_key
          vendor/bin/dep deploy production --ssh-key=/tmp/deploy_key
entries.bad_pattern:
# Anti-patterns the book calls out:

# 1. Believing CI "does everything automatically" — it only does what you wire up.
#    A "green" CI run does not mean everything is fine.
#    It means the jobs you defined passed. Wire in linting, tests, and build explicitly.

# 2. Secrets hardcoded in workflow YAML:
#    SSH_KEY: "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----..."
#    → always use secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY via the platform vault

# 3. Triggering deploy on every branch:
#    on: push
#    → production deploys must only come from main or release/* branches

# 4. Manual deployment via FTP after CI goes green:
#    → the pipeline should do the deploy; manual steps bypass the safety gates
entries.test_step: Check the CI config file (.github/workflows/ or .gitlab-ci.yml). Confirm deploy jobs only trigger on main or release/* branches, not on every push. Confirm all secrets (SSH key, host) are referenced via secrets.VARIABLE_NAME, not hardcoded. Confirm the workflow is committed to the repo and is not a manual external script.

entries.title: Linting and static analysis in CI — non-negotiable guardrails before every merge
entries.summary: "Looks good" is not a valid code check. A forgotten comma in an array once blocked an entire deployment because nobody had a linter. Linting and static analysis are not extras for big teams — they are the guardrails that keep you safe when it matters. Wire PHPCS (coding standard) and PHPStan or Psalm (type correctness, dead code, logic errors) into CI as non-negotiable steps. Define them as Composer scripts so every developer uses the same command. No push without checks.
entries.code_example:
// composer.json — define linting as a Composer script
{
  "scripts": {
    "lint":     "vendor/bin/phpcs --standard=WordPress src/",
    "lint:fix": "vendor/bin/phpcbf --standard=WordPress src/",
    "analyse":  "vendor/bin/phpstan analyse src/ --level=5"
  }
}

# .github/workflows/ci.yml — lint and static analysis as separate CI steps

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.2' }
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress
      - name: PHPCS — coding standard
        run: composer lint
      - name: PHPStan — static analysis
        run: composer analyse
entries.bad_pattern:
# Linting anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. No linter at all — relying on gut feeling:
#    → a forgotten comma, a wrong encoding, a broken style:
#    → "works on my machine" until it doesn't

# 2. Linting as part of a monolithic "composer ci" step:
#    → when CI goes red, nobody knows if it's the linter, the tests, or the build

# 3. Running the linter manually before pushing (not in CI):
#    → one developer forgets, a bad commit merges, the pipeline concept is broken

# 4. No PHPStan (only formatting checks):
#    → PHPCS catches style; PHPStan catches logic
#    → you need both
#    "Where your types don't match, where you're ignoring return values,
#     where you've built logic only you understand" — these are PHPStan territory
entries.test_step: Run `composer lint` and confirm PHPCS exits 0. Run `composer analyse` (or equivalent) and confirm PHPStan exits 0. Check the CI workflow — confirm linting runs as a named step separate from tests. Deliberately introduce a coding-standard violation and confirm CI catches it before the test step runs.

entries.title: Staging environment requirements — technically identical, logically independent
entries.summary: A good staging environment is more than a second domain or a cloned WordPress. It is based on the same codebase as production, deployed automatically from Git, has its own separate database and media, never sends emails to real users, and is password-protected or IP-restricted. Staging is your test track, your dress rehearsal, your safety net. If you develop on production, you are playing Russian roulette. The rule: live deployments never happen directly from a feature branch. Only merged, tested code from the main (or release) branch goes live.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml — automatic staging deploy on push

on:
  push:
    branches: [staging]

jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Composer dependencies
        run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress

      - name: Deploy to staging via Deployer
        env:
          SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.STAGING_SSH_KEY }}
        run: |
          echo "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > /tmp/staging_key
          chmod 600 /tmp/staging_key
          vendor/bin/dep deploy staging --ssh-key=/tmp/staging_key

# wp-config.php — staging-specific constants
# (set via environment, not committed to the repo)
#
# define('WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE', 'staging');
# define('WP_DEBUG', true);
# define('WP_DEBUG_LOG', true);
entries.bad_pattern:
# Staging anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Changes made locally → ZIP pushed to production → something breaks the frontend
#    → the client calls in a panic
#    This is the classic "no staging" disaster. Every change needs staging first.

# 2. Staging that still sends real emails:
#    → a test form submission notifies a real customer
#    → deactivate mail plugins or redirect all outbound email to Mailhog

# 3. Staging exposed to search engines:
#    → Google indexes the staging URL, duplicate content, SEO damage

# 4. Staging that shares the production database:
#    → a test that modifies data corrupts production content

# 5. Manual deploy steps to staging (FTP, ZIP upload):
#    → not reproducible, not reliable, introduces human error every time
entries.test_step: Check staging .env or wp-config.php — confirm WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE=staging or equivalent is set. Verify outbound email is intercepted (Mailhog or Disable Emails plugin active). Confirm robots.txt or meta robots contains noindex. Load staging.domain.com — it must require HTTP auth or be IP-restricted. Confirm the staging deploy is triggered by a push to the staging branch, not a manual step.

entries.title: Atomic deploy with symlinks — zero downtime, instant rollback
entries.summary: Professional deployment prepares each release outside the live path first. A release directory holds timestamped builds; a symlink named /current points to the active one. The new release is fully built — Composer, build scripts, file permissions, configuration — before the symlink is switched. No downtime, no race conditions. Rollback is one command: relink to the previous release. One WooCommerce project with a broken checkout template during a campaign launch was back online in 20 seconds this way — no panic, no SSH session.
entries.code_example:
# Symlink-based release deployment (shell, tool-agnostic)

RELEASES_DIR="/var/www/project/releases"
CURRENT_LINK="/var/www/project/current"
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
RELEASE_DIR="$RELEASES_DIR/$TIMESTAMP"

# 1. Create and populate the release directory
mkdir -p "$RELEASE_DIR"
rsync -az --exclude='.git' ./ "$RELEASE_DIR/"
cd "$RELEASE_DIR"
composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader
npm ci && npm run build

# 2. Link shared directories (uploads, .env, cache)
ln -nfs /var/www/project/shared/uploads  "$RELEASE_DIR/wp-content/uploads"
ln -nfs /var/www/project/shared/.env      "$RELEASE_DIR/.env"

# 3. Atomic symlink switch — zero downtime
ln -nfs "$RELEASE_DIR" "$CURRENT_LINK"

# 4. Clear cache, run health-check
php "$CURRENT_LINK/wp-cli.phar" cache flush
curl -sf https://example.com > /dev/null || (echo "Health check failed — rolling back" && ln -nfs "$RELEASES_DIR/previous" "$CURRENT_LINK")

# 5. Keep only the last 3 releases
ls -dt "$RELEASES_DIR"/* | tail -n +4 | xargs rm -rf
entries.bad_pattern:
# Deployment anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Deploying directly into the live directory:
#    rsync -az ./ /var/www/current/
#    → race condition: the site is in an inconsistent state during transfer
#    → an active request can load a mix of old and new PHP files

# 2. Writable cache directories inside the release:
#    /var/www/releases/20240724/wp-content/cache/
#    → after symlink switch, old cached HTML (e.g. a nav menu) is still served
#    → move cache dirs to shared/ and symlink them in

# 3. Not keeping old releases:
#    rm -rf /var/www/releases/*  # immediately after deploy
#    → rollback becomes a full DB restore and file re-upload instead of one command

# 4. Uploading wp-content/uploads/ as part of the release:
#    → uploads get wiped or overwritten on every deploy
#    → uploads must always be in shared/ and symlinked
entries.test_step: Check the server directory structure: confirm a releases/ directory with timestamped subdirectories and a current symlink. Run a deploy and confirm the symlink is switched as the last step (not during file transfer). Trigger a rollback and confirm the site is back on the previous release without a database restore. Confirm uploads/ and .env are symlinked from shared/, not copied into the release.

entries.title: Deployer for WordPress — PHP-based CLI deployment with stages, shared folders, and health checks
entries.summary: Deployer is PHP-based, CLI-driven, minimal, and stable. Used for 40+ projects including WordPress, Laravel, and APIs. A typical deploy.php includes stages for staging and production, SSH connections managed through secrets, shared folders for uploads, migrations, and health checks. Everything a deployment needs, without the overhead. Capistrano (Ruby-based) works but is unnecessarily complex without a Rails stack. Buddy looks nice but is UI-first — use plain text. Deployer is the right balance.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// deploy.php — minimal Deployer config for a WordPress project

namespace Deployer;

require 'recipe/common.php';

// ── Project config ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
set('repository', 'git@github.com:organisation/my-wp-project.git');
set('keep_releases', 3);

// Shared files/dirs — never inside a release directory.
set('shared_files', ['.env']);
set('shared_dirs', ['wp-content/uploads', 'wp-content/cache']);

// Dirs that must be writable by the web server.
set('writable_dirs', ['wp-content/uploads', 'wp-content/cache']);

// ── Hosts ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
host('staging')
    ->set('hostname', '{{STAGING_HOST}}')
    ->set('remote_user', 'deploy')
    ->set('deploy_path', '/var/www/staging')
    ->set('branch', 'staging');

host('production')
    ->set('hostname', '{{PROD_HOST}}')
    ->set('remote_user', 'deploy')
    ->set('deploy_path', '/var/www/production')
    ->set('branch', 'main');

// ── Custom tasks ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
task('wp:cache:flush', function () {
    run('cd {{release_path}} && php wp-cli.phar cache flush');
});

task('wp:health-check', function () {
    $url = get('public_url');
    $status = run("curl -sf -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' $url");
    if ($status !== '200') {
        throw new \RuntimeException("Health check failed — HTTP $status. Rolling back.");
    }
});

// ── Deploy flow ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
after('deploy:symlink', 'wp:cache:flush');
after('wp:cache:flush', 'wp:health-check');
after('deploy:failed', 'deploy:unlock');
entries.bad_pattern:
# Deployment tool anti-patterns:

# 1. Buddy (or any UI-first tool) as the sole deploy mechanism:
#    → deploy configuration lives in a UI, not in the repository
#    → new team members cannot see the deploy config in code review
#    → "no extra clicks, no UI hacks" — the book is explicit

# 2. Running composer update in production (not composer install with a lockfile):
#    → production sees different versions than staging
#    → always deploy with the lockfile: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist

# 3. No health-check step after symlink switch:
#    → the cache may still serve old HTML (e.g. a menu that broke after the deploy)
#    → add a curl check immediately after switching the symlink

# 4. Shared folders not configured in Deployer:
#    → uploads/ is included in the release and overwritten on every deploy
#    → set('shared_dirs', ['wp-content/uploads']) is not optional
entries.test_step: Run `vendor/bin/dep deploy staging` and confirm the release directory structure (releases/ + current symlink). Confirm uploads/ and .env are symlinked from shared/, not copied into the release. Confirm the health-check step runs after the symlink switch and rolls back if the site returns a non-200. Run `vendor/bin/dep rollback staging` and confirm it relinks to the previous release.

entries.title: Asset build belongs in the release, never in the repo — npm run build in CI
entries.summary: Builds don't belong in the repo — but they must be part of the release. Projects taken over where the theme was pushed but nobody ran "npm run build" had an empty <head>, no CSS, no navigation. Build locally or in CI first. Only when everything runs clean, deploy. Append hashes to filenames (style.min.hash.css), generate a manifest.json loaded by the theme, and make sure devDependencies (like Stylelint) never get deployed. Never push theme changes without a fresh build.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml — build assets in CI before deploying

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install npm dependencies (production + dev for build)
        run: npm ci

      - name: Build assets
        run: npm run build
        # npm run build generates dist/ with hashed filenames and manifest.json

      - name: Install Composer dependencies (no dev)
        run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader

      - name: Write version tag
        run: |
          echo "{"version": "$(git describe --tags --always)", "commit": "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)", "date": "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"}" > release.json

      - name: Deploy via Deployer
        run: vendor/bin/dep deploy production
entries.bad_pattern:
# Asset build anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Committing dist/ files to Git:
#    git add dist/style.min.css
#    → merge conflicts on every feature branch
#    → dist/ is a generated artifact; .gitignore it

# 2. Not running the build before deploying:
#    → the theme was pushed, npm run build was not run
#    → result: empty <head>, no CSS, no navigation
#    → one push-to-prod without a build destroyed a live site for hours

# 3. Deploying devDependencies to production:
#    npm install  (not npm ci --omit=dev)
#    → Stylelint, Storybook, test tools bloat the production node_modules
#    → use npm ci --omit=dev or ensure devDependencies never reach the server

# 4. No content hashes on filenames:
#    style.min.css  (no hash)
#    → browsers cache the old file after deploy; users see broken styles
#    → hashed filenames (style.min.abc123.css) force a cache bust
entries.test_step: Check .gitignore — confirm dist/ is excluded from version control. Run `npm run build` locally and confirm it generates dist/ files with content hashes. Check the CI workflow — confirm `npm ci` and `npm run build` run before the deploy step. After deploying, load the site and check the network tab: confirm CSS/JS filenames include a hash. Confirm a release.json or release.txt with the Git tag is written to the server on each deploy.

entries.title: Mirroring live database to local — wp db export, scp, import, search-replace
entries.summary: Local projects that develop on fake or empty content produce bugs that only show up in production. Real pages, posts, settings, media, and users are what the client is actively working on. The sync workflow: export the DB on the live server with `wp db export`, pull with scp or rsync, import with `ddev import-db`, then always run `wp search-replace` to rewrite URLs. Never skip the search-replace — WordPress stores URLs deep inside block content, custom fields, shortcodes, and rewrite rules.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/sync-live.sh — pull live DB and media into local DDEV

set -euo pipefail

LIVE_USER="deploy"
LIVE_HOST="example.com"
LIVE_WEB_ROOT="/var/www/html"
LOCAL_DOMAIN="https://project.ddev.site"
LIVE_DOMAIN="https://example.com"

echo "==> Exporting live database..."
ssh "$LIVE_USER@$LIVE_HOST" "wp db export /tmp/live-db.sql --allow-root"

echo "==> Pulling database..."
scp "$LIVE_USER@$LIVE_HOST:/tmp/live-db.sql" /tmp/live-db.sql

echo "==> Importing into DDEV..."
ddev import-db --src=/tmp/live-db.sql

echo "==> Running search-replace..."
# Never overwrite guid — it is the canonical post identifier
ddev wp search-replace "$LIVE_DOMAIN" "$LOCAL_DOMAIN" --skip-columns=guid

echo "==> Syncing media..."
rsync -az --progress \
  "$LIVE_USER@$LIVE_HOST:$LIVE_WEB_ROOT/wp-content/uploads/" \
  ./wp-content/uploads/

echo "==> Deactivating mail plugins..."
ddev wp plugin deactivate mailpoet --allow-root 2>/dev/null || true

chmod +x bin/sync-live.sh
entries.bad_pattern:
# Content mirroring anti-patterns the book documents:

# 1. Importing without search-replace:
#    ddev import-db --src=live-db.sql
#    # → no search-replace
#    → all internal links still point to live domain
#    → broken links, 404s, inconsistent data in blocks and shortcodes

# 2. Skipping the guid column in the wrong direction:
#    ddev wp search-replace example.com project.ddev.site  (no --skip-columns=guid)
#    → guid is overwritten, breaking the canonical post identifier

# 3. Forgetting to deactivate mail plugins after import:
#    → a test that triggers a WooCommerce "order confirmed" hook
#    → sends a real confirmation email to a real customer

# 4. Editing content in DDEV and pushing it back to live:
#    → the sync is one-directional: live → local
#    → never push local DB changes back to the live server

# 5. Developing locally with empty CPTs or dummy menus:
#    → bugs that only appear with real content miss the development phase
#    → debug issues with real blocks, real permalinks, and real user roles
entries.test_step: Run `bash bin/sync-live.sh` on a fresh local DDEV project. Confirm the local site loads with real content and images. Confirm internal links resolve correctly (no live-domain URLs in the nav or block content). Run `ddev wp option get siteurl` — it must return the local domain, not the live domain. Confirm no outbound emails are sent during the sync (check Mailhog or similar).

entries.title: Live data safety locally — anonymize, block email, never test payment plugins
entries.summary: Once live data is in the local environment, three rules apply without exception: do not keep real passwords, respect GDPR (never test with real customer data without anonymizing), and never test real payment plugins locally. Mail plugins must be deactivated — one CI run that sent a "welcome" email to a real customer happened exactly this way. The wp_options table contains everything (URLs, plugin settings, theme options, site language) — after import it overwrites local configuration, so handle it deliberately.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Anonymize real customer data after importing the live database locally.
# Run AFTER ddev import-db and search-replace.

set -euo pipefail

echo "==> Anonymizing user data..."

# Replace real email addresses with example.com addresses
ddev wp user list --field=ID | while read USER_ID; do
  ddev wp user update "$USER_ID" \
    --user_email="user${USER_ID}@example.com" \
    --display_name="Test User ${USER_ID}" \
    --user_pass="$(openssl rand -base64 12)"
done

echo "==> Deactivating payment and mail plugins..."
ddev wp plugin deactivate woocommerce-gateway-stripe mailpoet mailchimp-for-woocommerce 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Setting WP to dev mode..."
ddev wp config set WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE local --type=constant

echo "==> Done. Local DB has anonymized users and no live payment/mail integrations."
entries.bad_pattern:
# Live data safety anti-patterns:

# 1. Keeping real customer passwords in the local DB:
#    → the live DB hash might be guessable
#    → reset all passwords immediately after import:
#    ddev wp user reset-password 1 2 3 ...

# 2. Leaving mail plugins active after import:
#    → test runs (PHPUnit hooks, WP-CLI scripts) trigger real outbound emails
#    → one "welcome" email to a real customer is one too many

# 3. Testing real payment integrations locally:
#    ddev wp option update woocommerce_stripe_settings '{"enabled":"yes","testmode":"no",...}'
#    → even "accidentally" completing a test order can charge a real card

# 4. Not anonymizing before sharing the DB with a new team member:
#    → GDPR violation: real names, real emails, real orders visible to anyone
#    → always run the anonymization script before sharing a DB dump
entries.test_step: After running the sync script, run `ddev wp user list --fields=user_email` — no real email domain (other than @example.com) should appear. Confirm the payment plugin is deactivated: `ddev wp plugin is-active woocommerce-gateway-stripe` must exit 1. Confirm WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE is set to local: `ddev wp config get WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE`. Send a test form submission — confirm it is caught by Mailhog and does not reach a real inbox.

entries.title: Rollback discipline — symlink-based, under 60 seconds, no SQL restore needed
entries.summary: Rollback does not mean frantically deleting files or restoring SQL backups. It means switching back to the last working state in seconds, without anyone noticing. The symlink approach: keep the last 2–3 releases, relink to the previous one, clear cache — done. A WooCommerce project with a broken checkout template during a campaign launch was back online in 20 seconds this way. The golden rule from the book: "Never deploy what you can't roll back."
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/rollback.sh — relink current to the previous timestamped release

set -euo pipefail

RELEASES_DIR="/var/www/project/releases"
CURRENT_LINK="/var/www/project/current"

# Find the two most recent releases
CURRENT=$(readlink "$CURRENT_LINK")
PREVIOUS=$(ls -dt "$RELEASES_DIR"/* | grep -v "$CURRENT" | head -1)

if [[ -z "$PREVIOUS" ]]; then
  echo "No previous release to roll back to." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Rolling back from $CURRENT to $PREVIOUS"
ln -nfs "$PREVIOUS" "$CURRENT_LINK"

echo "Flushing cache..."
php "$CURRENT_LINK/wp-cli.phar" cache flush --allow-root

echo "Rollback complete. Current: $(readlink $CURRENT_LINK)"
entries.bad_pattern:
# Rollback anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. The only rollback strategy is restoring a SQL backup:
#    mysqldump → restore → reconfigure
#    → 20 minutes minimum, data loss risk
#    → symlink rollback takes 20 seconds and loses nothing

# 2. Not keeping old releases:
#    ls -dt /var/www/releases/* | tail -n +2 | xargs rm -rf
#    → keeps only the current release, no rollback possible
#    → keep at least 2–3 releases (set('keep_releases', 3) in Deployer)

# 3. Rollback without clearing cache:
#    ln -nfs /previous /current
#    # no cache flush
#    → PHP opcache still serves compiled bytecode from the old release path
#    → users see the new symlink but old PHP execution

# 4. DB migration without a down script:
#    ALTER TABLE wp_posts ADD COLUMN new_col TEXT;
#    # no reverse migration
#    → code rollback works, schema stays at the new version
#    → the old release's code now hits a schema it was never designed for
entries.test_step: Run a deploy, then run `bash bin/rollback.sh`. Confirm the symlink now points to the previous release. Confirm the site responds correctly (home page loads, admin login works). Confirm the cache was flushed after the rollback. If a DB migration was part of the deploy — confirm a down script exists and test it.

entries.title: Change management for WordPress — feature flags, pilot groups, and blue-green deploys
entries.summary: WordPress projects rarely fail because of the code itself. The real risk is in the rollout. A new theme, an integration, or swapping out a plugin won't crash a project — if it's introduced in a structured way. Change management means shaping deployments so they are controlled, testable, and always reversible. Three patterns: feature flags (ship the code, hide the feature until stable), pilot groups (internal team or 5% of users first, then everyone), blue-green deployment (old production stays live while the new version is tested, traffic switches when stable).
entries.code_example:
<?php
// Feature flag implementation — simple constant-based approach.
// The code ships to production; the feature is hidden until the flag is enabled.

// In wp-config.php (per environment):
// define('FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT', false);  // staging: true, production: false initially

// In plugin code:
function maybe_load_new_checkout(): void {
    if (!defined('FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT') || !FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT) {
        return;
    }
    add_action('woocommerce_checkout_init', 'new_checkout_init');
}
add_action('init', 'maybe_load_new_checkout');

// Pilot group via user role or meta:
function is_pilot_user(): bool {
    $user = wp_get_current_user();
    return in_array('pilot_tester', (array) $user->roles, true)
        || (bool) get_user_meta($user->ID, '_pilot_group', true);
}

function maybe_show_new_editor(): void {
    if (!is_pilot_user()) {
        return;
    }
    // Load the new editor for pilot users only.
    add_action('admin_enqueue_scripts', 'new_editor_scripts');
}
add_action('admin_init', 'maybe_show_new_editor');
entries.bad_pattern:
# Change management anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Everything goes live at once — no feature flags:
#    → a broken new checkout affects 100% of customers immediately
#    → ship the code, hide the feature behind a flag, enable gradually

# 2. All users are testers — no pilot group:
#    → a new editorial plugin was released to all 300 editors simultaneously
#    → support inbox overloaded in the first hour
#    → start with 5 internal editors, refine, then roll out

# 3. No rollback plan — nothing can be reversed:
#    → old theme was deleted before the new one was confirmed stable
#    → switching back required a full restore from backup (3 hours of downtime)
#    → keep old theme/plugin installed until the new version is verified stable

# 4. Chaos deployments — changes pushed live without tests, without rollback options:
#    → downtime, frustrated clients, expensive damage control
#    → "Changes aren't the real risk. Lack of change management is." (the book's conclusion)
entries.test_step: For any major change (new theme, new plugin, API swap): confirm a feature flag or pilot group is in place before the deploy. Confirm the old system remains available as a fallback for a defined transition period. Confirm DB migrations include a down script. After the pilot phase, confirm the rollout log includes feedback from pilot users before the full release. Document the rollout decision in a RELEASE.md or changelog.

entries.title: APM over uptime checks — trace where time goes per PHP function, DB query, and external call
entries.summary: Uptime monitoring only checks whether the server answers. APM (Application Performance Monitoring) tells you where the time actually goes — from the first millisecond to the last byte. A project can return HTTP 200 for an empty page while checkout is completely broken because an external API call is blocked. Without APM you will not notice until complaints arrive. New Relic provides continuous transaction tracking (PHP, MySQL, hooks); Blackfire is the targeted profiler for staging — visual call stacks, I/O wait, bottlenecks per function call. Both belong in a professional WordPress setup.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// Name a WP hook transaction in New Relic so it appears separately in the APM UI.
// Add to an MU-plugin or theme functions.php.

add_action('init', static function (): void {
    if (function_exists('newrelic_name_transaction')) {
        // Gives every request a meaningful name in the New Relic dashboard,
        // instead of lumping everything under "index.php".
        newrelic_name_transaction(
            is_admin() ? 'wp-admin/' . basename($_SERVER['SCRIPT_NAME'] ?? '') : get_queried_object_id() . '/' . get_post_type()
        );
    }
});
entries.test_step: Install New Relic PHP agent on staging. Load the homepage and the checkout page. Open the New Relic APM dashboard and confirm transactions are named (not all "index.php"). Sort by slowest transaction time and confirm the top-3 slow calls are either DB queries or external API calls, not unidentified. Add a deliberate slow external call (sleep) and confirm it shows up in the trace.

entries.title: Three-layer caching strategy — object cache (Redis), page cache, edge cache (CDN)
entries.summary: Caching is architecture, not a plugin you install and forget. Three distinct layers work together: Object cache (Redis or Memcached) keeps DB query results in memory so the same wp_options and menu queries are not recalculated on every request. Page cache stores complete HTML so PHP and MySQL are bypassed entirely for anonymous visitors. Edge cache (CDN — Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai) moves content close to visitors and filters DDoS/bot traffic. Cache strategy fails when dynamic pages are accidentally cached (users see other people's carts), or when edge and page cache invalidation are not aligned. A fashion shop that survived Instagram spikes reduced TTFB from 800 ms to 90 ms with Redis + Nginx FastCGI cache + Cloudflare full-page cache for anonymous users.
entries.test_step: Load the home page as an anonymous user and check X-FastCGI-Cache (or CF-Cache-Status for Cloudflare) — it must return HIT on the second request. Load the cart page — it must return MISS or BYPASS. Log in as a user and load the home page — it must return MISS or BYPASS. After a deploy, check TTFB on the first anonymous request: if the warm-up is in place, TTFB must be under the cold-cache threshold.

entries.title: WordPress Heartbeat — reduce frequency or disable on the frontend to cut admin-ajax.php load
entries.summary: The Heartbeat API sends AJAX requests to admin-ajax.php every 15–60 seconds for autosave, post-locking, and session handling. Five logged-in editors generate 20–40 extra requests per minute. Each request fully loads WordPress including plugins. On shared hosting or under traffic spikes, these requests block PHP workers and slow down frontend delivery. Fix: reduce frequency to 60 s or more, disable entirely on the frontend unless needed (WooCommerce stock updates), and limit to the specific backend screens that require it. Done with an MU-plugin or WP Rocket's Heartbeat control feature.
entries.code_example:
<?php
/**
 * MU-plugin: Heartbeat control.
 * Reduce backend frequency to 60 s; disable on the frontend entirely.
 * Drop in wp-content/mu-plugins/heartbeat-control.php
 */

add_filter('heartbeat_settings', static function (array $settings): array {
    // Reduce backend autosave interval to 60 seconds (default: 15–60).
    $settings['interval'] = 60;
    return $settings;
});

add_action('init', static function (): void {
    // Disable Heartbeat on the frontend completely.
    // Remove the condition if WooCommerce cart refresh is required.
    if (!is_admin()) {
        wp_deregister_script('heartbeat');
    }
});
entries.test_step: Open the WordPress admin with 2–3 tabs and run `watch -n 5 "grep admin-ajax /var/log/nginx/access.log | tail -20"` on the server. Confirm requests appear every 15 s before the fix and every 60 s after applying the MU-plugin. Load the frontend as an anonymous user and confirm no Heartbeat request goes to admin-ajax.php (no `action=heartbeat` in the network tab).

entries.title: Security hardening baseline — reduce attack surface from day one, not after a breach
entries.summary: Most WordPress compromises use automated bots scanning for basic negligence: weak passwords, unprotected admin login, outdated plugins. Security hardening starts by reducing the attack surface before reaching for a plugin. From day one: remove unused plugins and themes, disable the built-in file editor (DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT), restrict XML-RPC and REST API if not needed, protect wp-config.php and .env, allow SSH only via key-based auth. Admin rights are rare — anyone who has them must use 2FA (mandatory). Individual user accounts only, no shared logins. Dormant accounts removed immediately. WPScan runs automatically in CI after every staging deploy; a breach in the scan fails the build.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// wp-config.php — security hardening constants.
// Add these above the "That's all, stop editing!" line.

// Disable the theme/plugin file editor in wp-admin.
define('DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true);

// Disable unauthentic REST API access (non-logged-in users get 401).
// Remove if the project legitimately exposes public REST routes.
add_filter('rest_authentication_errors', static function ($result) {
    if (!empty($result)) {
        return $result;
    }
    if (!is_user_logged_in()) {
        return new WP_Error(
            'rest_not_logged_in',
            __('REST API access restricted.'),
            ['status' => 401]
        );
    }
    return $result;
});

// Disable XML-RPC entirely (only if no Jetpack / app that needs it).
add_filter('xmlrpc_enabled', '__return_false');
entries.test_step: Check wp-config.php: confirm DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT is defined as true. Open wp-admin → Appearance/Plugins — confirm the Editor menu item is gone. Make an unauthenticated REST API request to /wp-json/wp/v2/users — confirm it returns 401 if the project does not need public REST access. Run WPScan on the staging URL and confirm it exits 0 (no known vulnerabilities). SSH to the server and confirm PasswordAuthentication is disabled.

entries.title: Logging and alerting — capture errors, route to Slack, separate log categories, rotate
entries.summary: A WooCommerce shop can go silent for two weeks — no orders processed — while monitoring shows green, because an API timeout in checkout fails quietly with no alerts. Three steps are enough for any project size: Capture (WP_DEBUG_LOG to a custom log file), Store (separate error log from security log from custom application log), Alert (Slack webhook for critical errors — the team knows before the client does). Logs must be separated by category, rotated so they don't reach gigabytes, and never stored only locally (useless on production). Alerts via email are too easily lost; route critical events to Slack or Pushover directly.
entries.code_example:
<?php
/**
 * MU-plugin: Separate application event logging with Slack alert on critical errors.
 * Monolog is assumed (composer require monolog/monolog).
 * Drop in wp-content/mu-plugins/app-logging.php
 */

use Monolog\Logger;
use Monolog\Handler\StreamHandler;
use Monolog\Handler\SlackWebhookHandler;

add_action('plugins_loaded', static function (): void {
    if (!class_exists(Logger::class)) {
        return;
    }

    $log = new Logger('my-site');

    // Error log: PHP errors, DB errors, API failures.
    $log->pushHandler(new StreamHandler(WP_CONTENT_DIR . '/logs/error.log', Logger::ERROR));

    // Critical events also go to Slack.
    $slackUrl = defined('SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL') ? SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL : '';
    if ($slackUrl) {
        $log->pushHandler(new SlackWebhookHandler($slackUrl, null, null, true, null, false, false, Logger::CRITICAL));
    }

    // Expose via a simple helper so other code can log without importing Monolog directly.
    if (!function_exists('site_log')) {
        function site_log(string $message, array $context = [], string $level = 'error'): void {
            // Use error_log() as a lightweight fallback without Monolog.
            error_log('[' . strtoupper($level) . '] ' . $message . ' ' . wp_json_encode($context));
        }
    }
});
entries.test_step: Check wp-config.php: confirm WP_DEBUG_LOG is true and WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY is false. Trigger a deliberate error (call an undefined function) and confirm it appears in wp-content/debug.log (or the custom log path). Confirm the log is NOT accessible from the browser (the web server must deny access to wp-content/*.log). If Slack alerting is configured, trigger a CRITICAL-level log entry and confirm a Slack message arrives.

entries.title: Backup and disaster recovery — offsite storage, tested restores, tiered recovery runbook
entries.summary: A backup stored on the same server is a false sense of security — if the server fails, the backup is gone with it. A complete WordPress backup includes three parts: files (core + wp-content + wp-config.php / .env), database (all tables including custom prefixes), and optionally the server environment (PHP version, Nginx config, cron jobs). At minimum two physically separate storage locations are required, with at least one offsite (AWS S3, Backblaze B2, Google Cloud Storage) in a different region. A DR plan must answer: what gets backed up, how often, and how fast can the site be restored. Restore tests must be practiced quarterly on staging — not just "the restore completes" but "login, navigation, forms, and checkout work."
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Automated daily backup: DB export + file archive + offsite sync to S3.
# Runs via system cron: 0 2 * * * /path/to/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/wp-backup.log 2>&1

set -euo pipefail

WP_ROOT="/var/www/html"
BACKUP_DIR="/var/backups/wp-$(date +%F)"
S3_BUCKET="s3://your-bucket/wp-backups"

mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

echo "[backup] Starting WordPress backup at $(date)"

# 1. DB dump via WP-CLI.
wp --path="$WP_ROOT" db export "$BACKUP_DIR/db.sql" --allow-root
echo "[backup] DB export done"

# 2. Archive wp-content (themes, plugins, uploads).
tar -czf "$BACKUP_DIR/wp-content.tar.gz" "$WP_ROOT/wp-content"
echo "[backup] wp-content archive done"

# 3. Archive config files (never store secrets in the backup if they are in .env).
cp "$WP_ROOT/wp-config.php" "$BACKUP_DIR/"
echo "[backup] config backup done"

# 4. Sync to S3 (requires aws CLI configured with an IAM role or key).
aws s3 sync "$BACKUP_DIR/" "$S3_BUCKET/$(date +%F)/" --sse AES256
echo "[backup] S3 sync done"

# 5. Keep only the last 30 local backups.
ls -dt /var/backups/wp-* | tail -n +31 | xargs rm -rf
echo "[backup] Cleanup done"

# Restore test: (run monthly in CI or staging cron)
# wp db import /var/backups/wp-2025-08-17/db.sql --allow-root --skip-plugins --skip-themes
entries.test_step: Run the backup script on staging and confirm all three artifacts are created (db.sql, wp-content.tar.gz, wp-config.php). Confirm the S3 sync succeeds and the files appear in the bucket. Practice a DB-only restore: `wp db import db.sql --allow-root --skip-plugins --skip-themes`. After the import, confirm the staging site loads, you can log in, and the homepage content matches the dump date.

entries.title: Performance budgets — hard limits wired into CI so a breach fails the build
entries.summary: Performance always drifts. Editors upload larger images, plugins get added, databases grow. A site that shipped at 1.8 s LCP can be at 4.5 s a year later without anyone breaking anything intentionally. Performance budgets are hard numbers written down and enforced in CI. From the book: TTFB (warm cache hit) ≤ 500 ms, TTFB (cold/empty cache) ≤ 1.2 s, queries per request ≤ 60 on archive pages and ≤ 30 on detail pages, Redis hit rate ≥ 85%, autoload size ≤ 1 MB. When a budget trips, the build fails — no debate. Put budgets in the Definition of Done and run a short performance pass each quarter.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/perf-budget.yml — query-count budget check
# Runs a warm request and fails if the DB query count exceeds the budget.

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, staging]

jobs:
  performance-budget:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check query count on homepage
        run: |
          # Requires the staging URL to be queryable and Query Monitor to expose an HTTP header.
          QUERY_COUNT=$(curl -s -I "https://staging.example.com/?qm=1" | grep -i 'x-query-count' | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '\r')
          BUDGET=60
          if [ -z "$QUERY_COUNT" ]; then
            echo "Warning: could not read X-Query-Count header — skipping budget check"
            exit 0
          fi
          echo "Query count: $QUERY_COUNT (budget: $BUDGET)"
          if [ "$QUERY_COUNT" -gt "$BUDGET" ]; then
            echo "FAIL: query count $QUERY_COUNT exceeds budget of $BUDGET"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "PASS"
entries.test_step: Set a deliberate budget (e.g., ≤ 60 queries on the homepage). Open Query Monitor on staging after a real content import. Confirm the homepage is under budget. Introduce a test plugin that runs an unbounded WP_Query and confirm the CI budget check catches it. After removing the test plugin, confirm the check passes again.

entries.title: System cron over WP-Cron — reliable scheduled tasks independent of traffic
entries.summary: WP-Cron is built into WordPress Core, but it fires only when a visitor hits the site and can trigger right in the middle of critical processes. On low-traffic sites, scheduled tasks are delayed indefinitely. On high-traffic sites, multiple requests can all trigger the same event simultaneously. System cron (crontab) runs independently of traffic, guarantees execution at the scheduled time, and gives full control over logging and resource management. The migration is two steps: disable WP-Cron in wp-config.php and add a system cron job that calls wp-cron.php or the WP-CLI cron runner on the configured interval. In multi-server environments, use distributed locks (Redis locks or a jobs table) to prevent duplicate executions.
entries.code_example:
# System crontab for WordPress — replaces WP-Cron.
# Edit with: crontab -e -u www-data

# Run WordPress scheduled events every minute via WP-CLI.
# Prerequisites: DISABLE_WP_CRON defined in wp-config.php.
* * * * * /usr/local/bin/wp --path=/var/www/html cron event run --due-now --quiet >> /var/log/wp-cron.log 2>&1

# Separate weekly maintenance playbook: backup, optimize DB, flush old transients.
0 3 * * 0 /var/www/html/bin/maintenance.sh >> /var/log/wp-maintenance.log 2>&1

# Daily cache pre-warm after overnight content updates.
0 6 * * * /var/www/html/bin/cache-warm.sh >> /var/log/wp-cache-warm.log 2>&1
entries.test_step: Add `define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);` to wp-config.php. Run `wp cron test` — it must return "Success: WP-Cron spawning is disabled." Set up the system cron entry and run it manually: `wp --path=/var/www/html cron event run --due-now`. Confirm an expected event (e.g., wp_scheduled_delete) ran by checking `wp cron event list`. Check /var/log/wp-cron.log for the run record.

entries.title: WP-CLI automation playbooks — bundle maintenance tasks, version-control scripts, integrate into CI
entries.summary: A playbook is a documented routine — versioned, reproducible, and faster than clicking through admin menus. The daily maintenance playbook from the book completes in four minutes what used to take thirty. Scripts are stored in bin/ inside the project, version-controlled alongside the code, reviewed in pull requests like any other module, and integrated into CI/CD pipelines. Security ground rules for automation: use dedicated service accounts for cron jobs, API keys only for scheduled tasks with rotation and expiry dates, never store sensitive data in logs, and alert the team via Slack whenever a job fails.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/maintenance.sh — daily WordPress maintenance playbook.
# Run via system cron: 0 3 * * * /var/www/html/bin/maintenance.sh >> /var/log/wp-maintenance.log 2>&1

set -euo pipefail

WP="wp --path=/var/www/html --allow-root"
SLACK_WEBHOOK="${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL:-}"
LOG_PREFIX="[maintenance $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')]"

notify_slack() {
    local msg="$1"
    if [ -n "$SLACK_WEBHOOK" ]; then
        curl -s -X POST "$SLACK_WEBHOOK" \
          -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
          --data "{"text":"$msg"}" > /dev/null
    fi
}

echo "$LOG_PREFIX Starting"

# 1. Health check: abort if the site is unreachable.
HTTP_STATUS=$(curl -so /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://${SITE_DOMAIN:-example.com}/")
if [ "$HTTP_STATUS" != "200" ]; then
    notify_slack ":red_circle: Maintenance aborted: site returned HTTP $HTTP_STATUS"
    exit 1
fi

# 2. Delete post revisions older than 30 days.
$WP post delete $($WP post list --post_type=revision --date_query[before]="30 days ago" --format=ids) \
    --force 2>/dev/null || true

# 3. Delete expired transients.
$WP transient delete --expired

# 4. Optimize the DB.
$WP db optimize --quiet

# 5. Flush the object cache.
$WP cache flush

echo "$LOG_PREFIX Done"
notify_slack ":white_check_mark: Daily maintenance complete on ${SITE_DOMAIN:-example.com}"
entries.test_step: Run `bash bin/maintenance.sh` on staging. Confirm it completes without errors and logs output to the log file. Confirm expired transients were deleted: `wp transient list --expired` must return 0. Confirm revisions older than 30 days were deleted. Introduce a deliberate failure (set SITE_DOMAIN to a non-existent URL) and confirm the Slack alert fires.

entries.title: Hosting model and server configuration — PHP OPcache, MySQL buffer pool, Redis namespaces
entries.summary: Infrastructure is the stage for your code — if the stage shakes, even the best script looks bad. Plan hosting for the load in 18–24 months, not just today. The book's rules: always use the latest stable PHP version (7.4 → 8.2 is up to 20% faster); enable and fine-tune OPcache; set MySQL/MariaDB innodb_buffer_pool_size to 50–70% of RAM and enable the slow query log; use Redis namespaces for Multisite/WPML (blog_{id}_locale_{lang}_key) and monitor memory with INFO memory. Providers that lock core files, hide configurations, or restrict cron/shell access are deal breakers for professional projects.
entries.code_example:
; /etc/php/8.2/fpm/conf.d/99-opcache.ini
; OPcache settings for a production WordPress installation.

opcache.enable=1
opcache.enable_cli=0
; Memory for the compiled scripts. Increase for large sites with many plugins.
opcache.memory_consumption=256
; Maximum number of files to cache. Default (10000) is too low for WooCommerce + plugins.
opcache.max_accelerated_files=20000
; Check file timestamps on every request in development; disable in production for max speed.
opcache.validate_timestamps=0
; How often (seconds) to revalidate. 0 = never revalidate unless opcache.validate_timestamps=1.
opcache.revalidate_freq=0
; Interned strings memory. Useful for sites with many hooks and large plugin lists.
opcache.interned_strings_buffer=16
; Save comments (required by some WP plugins using PHPDoc annotations).
opcache.save_comments=1
entries.test_step: Run `php -i | grep opcache.enable` on the server — must return 1. Run `php -i | grep opcache.max_accelerated_files` — must be ≥ 20000 for a large WP install. Check MySQL: `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE "innodb_buffer_pool_size"` — confirm it is 50–70% of the server RAM. Check Redis: `redis-cli INFO memory | grep used_memory_human` and confirm it is within limits. Check Redis hit rate: `redis-cli INFO stats | grep keyspace_hits` vs. `keyspace_misses` — hit rate must be ≥ 85%.

entries.title: wp_options autoload bloat — audit options > 200 KB, set autoload=no for non-critical data
entries.summary: Every WordPress request loads all wp_options rows where autoload="yes" into memory before a single line of theme or plugin code runs. WordPress itself is lean; plugins are not. A weather API plugin caching 2.6 MB of response data in an autoloaded option will slow every admin page load, not just the weather widget. The book's case: an editorial team's "All Posts" load time went from 8–12 s to 1.8–2.4 s by moving 2.6 MB of API blobs (autoload → no) and shifting external API checks to WP-Cron. Rule: review everything above 500 KB. Save non-critical data with autoload="no".
entries.code_example:
<?php
/**
 * MU-plugin: External API result cached in wp_options with autoload=no.
 * The check runs via WP-Cron, not on every admin request.
 */

// Cron hook: runs once daily.
add_action('my_plugin_daily_api_check', static function (): void {
    $response = wp_remote_get('https://api.example.com/status', ['timeout' => 10]);
    if (is_wp_error($response)) {
        return;
    }
    // Store the result with autoload=no — will NOT be loaded on every request.
    update_option('my_plugin_api_status', wp_remote_retrieve_body($response), false);
});

// Register the daily cron event on plugin activation.
add_action('init', static function (): void {
    if (!wp_next_scheduled('my_plugin_daily_api_check')) {
        wp_schedule_event(time(), 'daily', 'my_plugin_daily_api_check');
    }
});

// Use the cached result without triggering a live API call.
function my_plugin_get_api_status(): string {
    return (string) get_option('my_plugin_api_status', '');
}
entries.test_step: Run the autoload audit query: `SELECT option_name, LENGTH(option_value) AS size_bytes FROM wp_options WHERE autoload = "yes" ORDER BY size_bytes DESC LIMIT 10`. If any row exceeds 500 KB, investigate what data it stores. Set that option to autoload=no: `wp option update <option_name> "$(wp option get <option_name>)" --autoload=no`. Reload the admin "All Posts" page and measure the time before and after.

entries.title: Daily health check routine — availability, security, backup status, error logs in 5–10 minutes
entries.summary: A WordPress site can run perfectly overnight and still be broken in the morning. A plugin update may have failed, a cron job didn't fire, an API went down, or a backup job stopped silently. The book's daily check covers four areas in 5–10 minutes: Availability and performance (monitoring dashboard — is the site online, is TTFB within normal range, any spikes in the last 24 h?); Security (Wordfence or WPScan — unusual login attempts, blocked IPs, unexpected file changes); Backup status (last backup created successfully? accessible? stored offsite?); Error logs (new PHP errors, DB issues, API timeouts). Ten minutes every morning prevents hours of damage control.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/daily-health-check.sh — morning health check script.
# Outputs a structured summary. Route the output to Slack via cron for passive monitoring.
# Cron: 0 7 * * * /var/www/html/bin/daily-health-check.sh | /var/www/html/bin/notify-slack.sh

set -euo pipefail

WP="wp --path=/var/www/html --allow-root"
SITE_URL="${SITE_URL:-https://example.com}"

echo "=== Daily health check: $(date) ==="

# 1. Availability check.
HTTP_STATUS=$(curl -so /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$SITE_URL")
echo "[availability] HTTP status: $HTTP_STATUS"

# 2. Check the last scheduled cron event ran successfully.
LAST_CRON=$($WP cron event list --format=json | python3 -c "import sys, json; events=json.load(sys.stdin); print(min(e['timestamp'] for e in events) if events else 'none')" 2>/dev/null || echo "error")
echo "[cron] Next scheduled event: $LAST_CRON"

# 3. Count PHP errors in the log from the last 24 hours.
LOG_FILE="${WP_CONTENT_DIR:-/var/www/html/wp-content}/debug.log"
if [ -f "$LOG_FILE" ]; then
    ERROR_COUNT=$(awk -v d="$(date -d '24 hours ago' '+%d-%b-%Y')" '$0 ~ d' "$LOG_FILE" | wc -l)
    echo "[errors] PHP log entries (last 24h): $ERROR_COUNT"
fi

# 4. Check backup age (file-based; adjust for your backup tool).
BACKUP_DIR="/var/backups"
LATEST_BACKUP=$(ls -t "$BACKUP_DIR"/wp-* 2>/dev/null | head -1 || echo "none")
echo "[backup] Latest backup directory: $LATEST_BACKUP"

echo "=== End of health check ==="
entries.test_step: Run `bash bin/daily-health-check.sh` on staging. Confirm it outputs an HTTP status of 200. Confirm the cron section reports a scheduled event. Confirm the backup section reports a backup directory from the last 24 hours. Simulate an error (trigger a PHP notice) and confirm it appears in the error count. Route the script output to Slack and confirm the message arrives.

entries.title: Crisis management runbook — detect, respond, recover, follow-up for WordPress incidents
entries.summary: Crises are not special cases — they are part of every project. Teams without a plan improvise, waste time, and lose trust. A prepared team works with a runbook: monitoring sounds the alarm (not the client), roles are defined (incident commander makes decisions, technical team follows the runbook, communications updates the client on a fixed schedule), and every incident ends with a post-mortem. A compromised WordPress site is cleaned by procedure: maintenance mode → kill sessions → change all passwords → reinstall core → compare plugins and themes → scan uploads for PHP files → review wp_options and cron events → restore from a clean backup if uncertain. Without follow-up, crises are wasted time.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/incident-response.sh — minimal compromised site first-response script.
# Run after confirming a compromise. Requires root/sudo on the server.

set -euo pipefail

WP="wp --path=/var/www/html --allow-root"
SLACK_WEBHOOK="${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL:-}"

notify() {
    local msg="$1"
    echo "[incident] $msg"
    if [ -n "$SLACK_WEBHOOK" ]; then
        curl -s -X POST "$SLACK_WEBHOOK" \
          -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
          --data "{"text":":rotating_light: INCIDENT: $msg"}" > /dev/null
    fi
}

notify "Starting incident response at $(date)"

# Step 1: Maintenance mode on (wp maintenance-mode ships with modern WP-CLI; on old versions drop a .maintenance file in the web root).
$WP maintenance-mode activate 2>/dev/null || true
notify "Maintenance mode activated"

# Step 2: Kill all active sessions.
$WP user session destroy --all
notify "All user sessions destroyed"

# Step 3: Reinstall WordPress core (does NOT overwrite wp-config.php).
$WP core download --force
notify "WordPress core reinstalled"

# Step 4: Scan uploads for PHP files (should be zero — PHP in uploads = backdoor).
PHP_IN_UPLOADS=$(find /var/www/html/wp-content/uploads -name "*.php" | wc -l)
if [ "$PHP_IN_UPLOADS" -gt "0" ]; then
    notify "WARNING: $PHP_IN_UPLOADS PHP file(s) found in uploads — review immediately"
    find /var/www/html/wp-content/uploads -name "*.php" | tee /tmp/suspicious-uploads.txt
fi

# Step 5: List all cron events for manual review.
$WP cron event list --format=table > /tmp/cron-events-review.txt
notify "Cron event list saved to /tmp/cron-events-review.txt"

notify "First response steps complete. Manual steps required: change passwords, restore from backup if uncertain."
entries.test_step: Simulate a maintenance mode activation on staging: `wp maintenance-mode activate`. Confirm the site returns a maintenance page to anonymous visitors but wp-admin is still accessible. Run `wp user session destroy --all` and confirm you are logged out on all devices. Run `find wp-content/uploads -name "*.php"` — confirm 0 results on a clean install. Run `wp cron event list` and verify all scheduled events are expected.

entries.title: Distributed architecture — separate DB, cache, and storage from the web server from day one
entries.summary: A one-box setup runs everything on a single machine: web server, PHP, MySQL, cache, and uploads all share resources. When traffic spikes or one component fails, everything collapses. A fashion client's shop crashed 14 minutes into a campaign launch because the entire stack shared one power strip. Distributed architecture separates components so each can fail and be scaled independently. Even a single server can be "distributed in mindset" by running MariaDB in a separate container and storing uploads in S3-compatible storage. The cost delta is minimal; the operational flexibility is large.
entries.code_example:
# docker-compose.yml — minimal distributed WordPress stack on a single host.
# Separates PHP-FPM, MariaDB, and Redis into isolated containers.
# Uploads are expected to go to S3-compatible storage (configured in wp-config.php).

version: '3.9'

services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ['80:80', '443:443']
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - wp_files:/var/www/html:ro
    depends_on: [php]

  php:
    image: wordpress:php8.2-fpm
    environment:
      WORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db
      WORDPRESS_DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME}
      WORDPRESS_DB_USER: ${DB_USER}
      WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - wp_files:/var/www/html
    depends_on: [db, redis]

  db:
    # Separate container = separate resource limits; survives PHP restarts.
    image: mariadb:10.11
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: ${DB_NAME}
      MYSQL_USER: ${DB_USER}
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${DB_ROOT_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/mysql
    # Tune buffer pool to 50–70% of the RAM allocated to this container.
    command: --innodb-buffer-pool-size=512M

  redis:
    # Separate container = cache eviction never competes with DB connections.
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

volumes:
  wp_files:
  db_data:
entries.bad_pattern:
# One-box anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. All services on one machine, no separation:
#    Web server + PHP + MySQL + Redis + uploads all share the same CPU/RAM/disk.
#    → A traffic spike hits everything at once; one slow DB query stalls PHP workers
#      and blocks the web server.

# 2. Storing uploads locally (not offsite):
#    /var/www/html/wp-content/uploads/ — stored on the web server only.
#    → Horizontal scaling (adding a second web server) breaks because uploads
#      exist on only one server.
#    → Migrate to S3-compatible storage immediately; wp_get_attachment_url()
#      still works; only the storage location changes.

# 3. Waiting for traffic to grow before separating:
#    → Restructuring under load is risky and stressful.
#    → Separate components while the system is under no pressure.
entries.test_step: Run `docker compose ps` and confirm db, redis, and php are in separate containers. Confirm the database container has its own resource limits: `docker stats` — db memory usage must not affect php container CPU. Load the WordPress site, add a product to the cart, confirm the request completes normally. Check Redis hit rate: `docker exec <redis_container> redis-cli INFO stats | grep keyspace_hits` — should increment on repeated page loads.

entries.title: Enterprise caching strategy — edge TTLs, selective invalidation, cache warmup after deploys
entries.summary: Caching is not a plugin switch. It is a deliberate strategy covering three layers (edge/CDN, page cache, object cache) with rules about what gets cached, where, how long, and what triggers invalidation. Common mistakes: flushing the entire cache on every minor content update, and setting CDN TTLs at defaults too short to be useful. From the book: static assets baseline 4 hours, dynamic pages 5–15 minutes. Object cache hit rate below 90% is a red flag. A cache warmup job must run automatically after every deploy so the first real visitor never hits a cold cache.
entries.code_example:
# bin/cache-warm.sh — post-deploy cache warmup script.
# Crawls the sitemap and pre-loads pages before real traffic arrives.
# Add as a CI/CD post-deploy step: bash bin/cache-warm.sh

set -euo pipefail

SITE_URL="${SITE_URL:-https://example.com}"
SITEMAP_URL="${SITEMAP_URL:-${SITE_URL}/sitemap.xml}"
WARMUP_CONCURRENCY=4   # parallel curl jobs; tune for server capacity

echo "[cache-warm] Fetching sitemap from $SITEMAP_URL"

# Extract all <loc> URLs from the sitemap.
URLS=$(curl -s "$SITEMAP_URL" | grep -oP '(?<=<loc>)[^<]+' | head -200)
URL_COUNT=$(echo "$URLS" | wc -l)
echo "[cache-warm] Warming $URL_COUNT URLs with concurrency $WARMUP_CONCURRENCY"

# Warm in parallel. -s = silent, -o /dev/null discards body, -w prints status.
echo "$URLS" | xargs -P "$WARMUP_CONCURRENCY" -I{} sh -c   'STATUS=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "{}"); echo "[warm] {} -> $STATUS"'

echo "[cache-warm] Done"
entries.bad_pattern:
# Caching strategy anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Flushing the entire cache on every post save:
#    add_action('save_post', function() { wp_cache_flush(); });
#    → Every content update wipes all cached pages.
#    → The next N visitors all get cold cache; DB and PHP spike.
#    → Purge only the affected page + archives; leave unrelated pages warm.

# 2. CDN TTLs left at default (often 1 hour or less for HTML):
#    → Every page request that misses the CDN hits the origin.
#    → Review and increase TTLs. Static assets can be 1 week+ if versioned.

# 3. No cache warmup after deploy:
#    → A deploys at 9 AM → CDN, page cache, and object cache are all empty.
#    → 9–9:15 AM: every visitor pays full generation cost.
#    → Googlebot crawls exactly now: bad Core Web Vitals signals.
#    → Add a post-deploy warmup step to the CI/CD pipeline.

# 4. Object cache hit rate below 90% — never investigated:
#    → 40% of requests go straight to MySQL for the same menu and options query.
#    → Root cause: missing blog_id in Multisite cache keys; one-line fix.
entries.test_step: Run `bash bin/cache-warm.sh` on staging after a deploy. Confirm all URLs return HTTP 200. Load the homepage as anonymous user and check response headers: X-FastCGI-Cache or CF-Cache-Status must return HIT on the second request. Load the cart page and confirm it returns MISS or BYPASS. Check Redis hit rate after the warmup: `redis-cli INFO stats` — keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses) must be ≥ 90%.

entries.title: High-availability failover testing — kill each component under load to prove the HA setup works
entries.summary: HA diagrams always look great on paper. The real question is whether the system actually switches over when something breaks. Teams set up primary/replica databases, load-balanced web servers, and cache clusters — and then never test whether failover actually works. From the book: test each component independently by deliberately killing it under load. Kill the primary database and confirm the replica takes over. Pull a web server out of the load balancer and confirm others handle traffic. Shut down a cache node and confirm the secondary picks up. Run these drills under real load, not just in quiet conditions.
entries.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/failover-drill.sh — minimal HA component failover drill script.
# Run under simulated load (e.g., while ab or k6 is running against staging).
# Requires access to Docker or SSH on the target host.

set -euo pipefail

echo "=== HA Failover Drill: $(date) ==="

# --- 1. Cache node failover ---
echo "[drill] Stopping redis container to simulate cache node failure..."
docker stop redis-primary 2>/dev/null || true
sleep 5

echo "[drill] Checking cache hit rate via redis-secondary..."
docker exec redis-secondary redis-cli PING   # must return PONG

# Confirm the site still serves requests during the cache outage.
HTTP=$(curl -so /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "${SITE_URL:-https://staging.example.com}/")
echo "[drill] Site HTTP status during cache failure: $HTTP"

docker start redis-primary

# --- 2. Web server removal from load balancer ---
# (Conceptual; actual implementation depends on load balancer API — Nginx, HAProxy, cloud LB.)
echo "[drill] Removing web-2 from load balancer pool..."
# Example for Nginx upstream: edit upstream block or use nginx-plus API.
echo "[drill] Verify traffic routes to web-1 only — check access logs."

echo "=== Drill complete — review application errors above ==="
entries.bad_pattern:
# HA testing anti-patterns from the book:

# 1. Setting up HA and never testing it:
#    → Primary/replica database is configured; nobody has ever killed the primary.
#    → First real test happens during a production outage.
#    → Run a scheduled failover drill quarterly — the setup is only as good as the last test.

# 2. Testing only under quiet conditions:
#    → Failover works at 2 AM with no traffic.
#    → During a traffic peak (200 req/s), the 5-second health-check gap causes a visible error spike.
#    → Test under realistic load to expose timing-sensitive gaps.

# 3. Monitoring only uptime, not component-level metrics:
#    → Site shows 200 OK; nobody sees the cache hit rate dropped from 92% to 12%.
#    → DB query latency doubled; pages are slow but "the site is up."
#    → Add cache hit rate and DB latency to the monitoring dashboard.
entries.test_step: While a load test is running against staging (e.g., `ab -n 1000 -c 20 https://staging.example.com/`): stop the Redis container and confirm requests still complete (cold-cache fallback). Start Redis again. Pull one web server from the load balancer and confirm traffic routes correctly — check access logs on the remaining server. After each step, confirm HTTP 200 and no application errors in the log.

entries.title: Agency operations — ownership per module, unified CI/CD templates, and release trains
entries.summary: Enterprise and agency projects fail because of missing structure, not bad code. Three principles fix this: Ownership (every repo, module, and interface has a named owner — bugs stop bouncing; one intranet went from 5-day average resolution to under 24 hours after introducing ownership); Standards (all projects follow unified CI/CD templates, PHPStan Level 8, ESLint, mandatory Composer audit — one agency cut maintenance by 30% by centralizing pipeline templates); Release discipline (fixed schedule, code freeze the day before, smoke tests, client review window). Combine all three and even 20 parallel projects become manageable.
entries.code_example:
# .github/workflows/ci-unified.yml
# Unified CI template shared across all agency repos.
# Each project repo imports this via workflow_call or copies it from a central template repo.
# Enforces PHPStan, Composer audit, and automated tests on every PR.

name: Unified Agency CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, staging]

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up PHP
        uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: '8.2'
          coverage: none

      - name: Install Composer dependencies
        run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist

      # Standard: PHPStan Level 8 across all agency repos.
      - name: PHPStan static analysis
        run: vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --level=8 src/

      # Standard: Composer security audit — fail on known vulnerabilities.
      - name: Composer security audit
        run: composer audit --no-interaction

      # Standard: Unit tests with coverage threshold.
      - name: Run tests
        run: vendor/bin/phpunit --coverage-text

  # Wave rollout gate: smoke test before promoting to next wave.
  smoke-test:
    needs: quality
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Smoke test staging
        run: |
          STATUS=$(curl -so /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$STAGING_URL")
          if [ "$STATUS" != "200" ]; then exit 1; fi
          echo "Smoke test passed: HTTP $STATUS"
entries.test_step: Open the CI/CD pipeline for two different agency repos and confirm they share the same PHPStan level and Composer audit step. Introduce a known vulnerable package in composer.json on a test branch and confirm the CI audit step fails. Check each repo's README.md for an "Owner:" line. Verify that the most recent deploy happened on a scheduled release day, not ad-hoc.

entries.title: SEV matrix and incident runbooks — tiered response rules so every outage has a clear playbook
entries.summary: Even with strong structure, things go wrong. A SEV (severity) matrix defines response actions by incident type so there is no debate when something breaks — everyone knows exactly what to do. From the book: checkout down = immediate escalation and on-call; cron job stuck = fix within the same day; admin bug = fix in the next scheduled release. Runbooks complete the setup: short, clear step-by-step guides for recurring issues. Example: "Cron job stuck → check logs → trigger job manually → monitor." Without defined tiers and runbooks, every incident starts with a debate about priorities — exactly when clarity is most critical.
entries.code_example:
# docs/runbooks/cron-job-stuck.md — example runbook stored in the project repo.
# Versioned with code so it stays current.

# Runbook: Cron Job Stuck

## Symptoms
- Scheduled events not firing (emails not sent, stock not synced)
- wp-cron.log shows no entries for > 10 minutes
- WP CLI: `wp cron event list` shows past-due events
