## Response steps

1. Check cron log for errors:
   ```bash
   tail -50 /var/log/wp-cron.log
   ```

2. Confirm DISABLE_WP_CRON is set (system cron must be the trigger):
   ```bash
   wp config get DISABLE_WP_CRON
   # Expected output: true
   ```

3. Confirm the system crontab entry is active:
   ```bash
   crontab -l -u www-data | grep wp
   # Expected: * * * * * /usr/local/bin/wp ... cron event run --due-now
   ```

4. Manually run due events:
   ```bash
   wp --path=/var/www/html cron event run --due-now
   ```

5. Monitor next scheduled run:
   ```bash
   watch -n 60 'wp cron event list --format=table | head -20'
   ```

## Escalation
If step 4 fails with errors: SEV 1 → page on-call.
If step 4 succeeds: SEV 2 resolved → monitor + file a ticket to investigate root cause.
entries.test_step: Open the project docs and confirm a runbook exists for at least one recurring incident type (cron, deploy rollback, or cache flush). Deliberately stop the system cron and confirm the monitoring alert fires within 10 minutes. Run the cron runbook manually and confirm all steps complete without requiring knowledge not in the doc. Verify the post-mortem template exists in the repo.

entries.summary: In every WordPress project, content is the actual product. Default roles (Author, Editor, Administrator) are too coarse for teams of any size. entries.title: Multilingual translation workflow — one source language, TMS integration, and style guides
entries.summary: Multilingual publishing is a classic source of errors: translations start before the source is approved, terminology is inconsistent across markets, and stale translated content goes live when the original changes. From the book: one language is the source of truth; translations begin only after the original is approved; style guides enforce consistent terminology. WPML or Polylang Pro provides the WordPress-side workflow. Enterprise environments connect WordPress to external Translation Management Systems (Lokalise, Phrase, Crowdin) via API. Result for an international portal that implemented this: consistent messaging across all markets instead of per-country chaos.

entries.title: Team organization — tickets as single source of truth, mandatory code reviews, and docs-as-code
entries.summary: A project can be technically flawless and still sink when organization is missing. Symptoms: tickets vanish, communication spreads across ten channels, developers push directly to production, nobody knows what changed. From the book: four practices eliminate this. Tickets as the single source of truth (Jira or GitHub Issues with issue templates — one shop reduced average bugfix time from 3 days to 1 day by adding reproduction steps to templates). Mandatory code reviews (no merge without review, author never merges their own PR). Docs-as-code (Markdown files in the project repo, versioned with every commit). Short focused meetings (daily standup with 3 questions and a timer; release meeting is a confirmation, not a discussion).

entries.title: Onboarding and documentation — living docs with MkDocs, DocBlocks, and automated changelogs
entries.summary: In almost every WordPress project the day comes when nobody remembers why a decision was made. A developer leaves, a client asks about an old feature, a local environment needs to be set up, and the search begins through Slack chats and old PDFs. Documentation is not extra work — it is part of the software architecture. From the book: MkDocs turns Markdown files in the repo into a full searchable documentation site, versioned with every commit; one agency cut onboarding from two weeks to five days. DocBlocks explain the why, not the how. Short screencasts cover workflows that are easier shown than described. Automated changelogs via GitHub Actions and mikepenz/release-changelog-builder make releases transparent to both developers and clients.
entries.code_example:
# mkdocs.yml — MkDocs configuration for a WordPress project.
# Markdown docs live in docs/ inside the project repo.
# Run: mkdocs serve (local preview) or mkdocs gh-deploy (GitHub Pages).

site_name: My WordPress Project
site_url: https://yourdomain.github.io/my-wp-project/
docs_dir: docs/
theme:
  name: material   # pip install mkdocs-material
  palette:
    primary: indigo

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Setup: setup.md
  - Architecture: architecture.md
  - Deployment: deployment.md
  - Runbooks:
    - Cron job stuck: runbooks/cron-job-stuck.md
    - Cache flush: runbooks/cache-flush.md
  - Changelog: changelog.md

---
# .github/workflows/changelog.yml — automated changelog on release.

name: Release Changelog
on:
  release:
    types: [published]

jobs:
  changelog:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Build release changelog
        id: changelog
        uses: mikepenz/release-changelog-builder-action@v5
        with:
          configuration: .github/changelog-config.json
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Update CHANGELOG.md
        run: |
          echo "${{ steps.changelog.outputs.changelog }}" > /tmp/new-entry.md
          cat /tmp/new-entry.md CHANGELOG.md > /tmp/merged.md
          mv /tmp/merged.md CHANGELOG.md
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add CHANGELOG.md
          git commit -m "chore: update changelog for ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}"
          git push

Click the Setup and Architecture pages and confirm they render without broken links. Open a random PHP function in the codebase and confirm it has a DocBlock that explains the *why*, not just the *what*. Check CHANGELOG.md: confirm the last release entry was generated automatically (look for PR numbers and labels like "feature" or "fix").

entries.title: Knowledge retention — docs-as-code, pair programming, and ownership rotation prevent knowledge silos
entries.summary: Every project eventually faces the "bus factor" problem: a single developer holds critical knowledge in their head, leaves or is unavailable, and the team is stuck. From the book: three practices prevent silos. Docs-as-code (Markdown in the repo, versioned with every commit) makes knowledge durable and discoverable. Pair programming is the fastest knowledge transfer — two developers on the same feature may seem twice as expensive but produce fewer bugs, less support work, and faster future onboarding. Ownership rotation (every 6 months) ensures multiple team members understand each module. The book's case study: Team A barely documented; after 6 months nobody was sure which features were stable. Team B used MkDocs, DocBlocks, and automated changelogs — every feature had a clear trail; clients felt secure.

# docs/architecture.md — architecture decision record template.
# Store one ADR per significant decision in docs/adr/.
# Template from the book's "docs-as-code" practice.

# ADR-0012: Switched from WP-Cron to system cron

## Status
Accepted — 2026-05-14

## Context
WP-Cron fires only when a visitor hits the site. On our staging environment
(low traffic), scheduled imports were delayed by hours. On the production site
(high traffic), the same import was triggered multiple times simultaneously,
causing database deadlocks.

## Decision
Disable WP-Cron (DISABLE_WP_CRON = true in wp-config.php) and replace it
with a system crontab entry running WP-CLI every minute.

## Consequences
- Scheduled tasks now run at precise times, independent of traffic.
- Requires the system cron to be configured on every server (documented in setup.md).
- Multi-server environments need Redis-based distributed locks (see bin/cron-lock.sh).

## Owner
@alice (rotates to @bob on 2026-12-01)

# Every step documented so any new developer can onboard without asking.

- Docker Desktop >= 4.x
- WP-CLI installed globally (`brew install wp-cli`)
- Node 22 via nvm

```bash
git clone git@github.com:org/project.git && cd project
cp .env.example .env           # fill in DB credentials
docker compose up -d
wp core install --url=localhost --title="Local Dev" --admin_user=admin --admin_email=dev@example.com
wp plugin activate --all
```

```bash

npm run test:e2e
```
